Hon. GEO. E. FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved, that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Inspection and Sale Act, by providing that "binder twine manufactured for export only, and not to be used in Canada, need not be labelled with the name of the dealer and number of feet of twine per pound in the ball marked or stamped thereon, and that the minister may make regulations to prevent the sale or use in Canada of unlabelled binder twine manufactured for export only, and that any person violating such regulation shall be liable Vo a penalty.

What is the object of
the resolution?

The object really is. explained by the resolution itself. As the law is at present, all binder twine manufactured in Canada, whether for use in this country or for export, has to be labelled as set out in the resolution. The object of the Bill, which it is intended to introduce, is to make it possible that binder twine manufactured in this country for export only, not for use in the country, need not have that label; and that the minister may have power to make such regulations as are necessary to prevent any twine manufactured for export being sold within the bounds of Canada. The reason for it is that large orders come from foreign countries for binder twine, but they do not want the twine with any label or mark on it, and the fact that it has to be labelled and marked under our present law prevents the orders being placed in this country. It is to expedite manu-

facture in our own country for export, whilst at the same time maintaining every restriction necessary to prevent the sale of untagged binder twine within Canada.

My hon. friend then
admits that we do export binder twine? I heard an argument once in this House that any article which was manufactured and not really strongly protected stood a very poor show of having any export sale; and I am glad to hear that the export of binder twine is so great that we have to do something to meet the expanding market. I thought perhaps the intention was to meet the conditions where they have to have marks that we do not have.

I am delighted that my
hon. friend is delighted.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee on the resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

Would this not be rather an inducement to the manufacturers for export, to deceive? The minister guards against any deception at home, which I am glad of, but would not the rescinding of the regulations requiring branding of binder twine be rather an incentive to the manufacturer to deceive the foreign buyer? Has the department looked into that phase of the question?

Yes, so far as it is necessary. A buyer in foreign countries has his own views, his own tastes, maybe his own purposes. He is quite willing to place the order for goods if you put them up as he wishes as to marks. The object" of this legislation is to enable the foreign merchants to put their own marks on the binder twine. It would be easy to tear off the marks required under the Canadian law, but that would toe an expensive operation when the, balls are all done up in large cases. I think we go as far as necessary if we protect our own buyers and consumers, and allow those of other countries to protect themselves.

If the foreign buyer sells our binder twine as Canadian twine and puts a false mark on it, it may leave a bad impression as to Canadian manufacture. If he sells it as his own without any country of origin being marked on the twine, then no injury would be done.
That is his purpose; he does not want any mark on it to show the place of origin.

The binder twine
factory at Peterborough could not sell its twine in foreign countries if marked. The Russian importer would not take it if it was marked in any way, and it is to provide for that that this legislation is introduced.

I am a little afraid that this is general legislation to meet a special case, which is always dangerous. In the case of other articles of export we have passed drastic legislation as to marking so that the goods shall he identified as Canadian goods, and so that they shall be known to have a certain standard of quality.
I am quite aware that it would be dangerous to draw absolute, general conclusions from that particular instance; but it seems to me that under ordinary circumstances, if we are doing business on a proper basis, it must be in our interest that the world should know it, and that the people with whom we are doing business should have that assurance. ^ As to binder twine which is to be marketed and used in Canada, we have legislation providing for the marking of the length of the twine. That has been found absolutely necessary, and an active inspection has been instituted to see that that legislation is lived up to. It seems to me remarkable that what is found to be so urgently necessary in Canada should be so entirely objectionable in some other countries. I think that the minister would be well advised to take the matter into fuller consideration, possibly, than he has done, and not Test his case on the representation of a single twine factory, but rather take advice from all the twine factories, and then take into consideration all the general conditions as they would affect the interests of the country and its reputation. With all due respect to the manufacturing interests concerned, I am afraid that their suggestion has a very strong air of suspicion connected with it. I would be very much more in favour of a policy that would take every means to establish the quantity and quality of Canadian goods sold in foreign countries.

I proceeded on the exact lines that my hon. friend has laid down. I looked into this question thoroughly, and came to this conclusion after having given as full consideration as I thought was necessary to the subject. It is not a very abstruse one; I do not think there are any very great difficulties connected with it. In the first place, we inspect and mark not for
quality, but for the length of the twine in the ball. The primary object of the legislation was to protect the Canadian farmer against short lengths. He received his ball of binder twine; he could not unravel and measure it for himself, and this legislation was planned and placed on the statute book for the purpose of protecting him in that regard, and, I think, for that purpose only. I do not think the legislation had in view at all the protection of people of other countries. It seems to have been unnecessary at that time to do anything: else in the legislation than to protect our own people. However, that was the way the legislation went on the statute book, and that is the way it is to-day. If by this new legislation we absolutely protect' our own farmers, there is no fault to be found inside the boundaries of Canada. The same regulations will be effective,, there will be the same inspectors, the same inspection, and the same care will be taken, and therefore the same advantages will come to our own farmers. No other country in the world that I know of makes any provision having regard to the export sale of binder twine, as to whether the twine shall be of a certain quality or of a certain length. We were not, as in the case of butter, cheese and the like, trying to establish in outside countries the name of an article manufactured in Canada. The United States has nolegislation like this. Mfhen the Russian buyer comes into the market, he is willing to place an order in the Canadian factory, but the Canadian factory puts its own marks upon the goods. He says: I do not want any marks upon my twine; when it goes to Vladivostock or other ports, I put my own marks and tags upon it. But, says the Canadian manufacturer, the law prevents us from leaving them off. The Russian buyer accordingly gives the order to a United States firm; in one case an order was given to the United States partner of a firm here. Sometimes it is difficult to know why people respect certain marks and object to others, but that takes place in thousands of instances in the course of trade. It is a question of whether you are willing to cater to the desires of the buyer in the foreign country, or whether you are willing to lose the trade. We do all that is necessary when we take the proper steps to protect our own people. If, by taking this course, we can get more wages and more labour for our own people, I think we ought to do it, and that is the idea upon which I have taken action.

I am rather inclined to agree with the hon. Minister of Trade and v Commerce, for the reason he pointed out in his last few words. One of the difficulties complained of by our agents abroad is that the Canadian manufacturer does not yield sufficiently to the whims of his customers in foreign countries. If you wish to sell goods in South America, you have to manufacture and put them up the way the people an South America want them. Perhaps we prefer to follow our own inclinations and our own patterns, but the South American people will 'not have them, and it is just the same, I suppose, with countries that buy our twine. The invariable view of those who take an interest in the expansion of our trade is that one reason why that trade does not expand more rapidly is because the Canadian producer, particularly the manufacturer, is slow to yield to the desires of foieign customers. The trade cannot be got in that way; you have to meet the ideas of your customers. I am inclined to the belief that so long as the Canadian people are absolutely protected against fraud and get good value for their money, in order to expand our trade we ought to^ meet as far as possible the desires of tnose whom we are trying to get as purchasers. I am not sure that we are altogether responsible for what the Russian is going to do with his twine. He has his own way of doing business, and if he sells the twine to his customers as his own, we are not bound as a country or as a government to protect them. If we want to try to make a name for Canadian twine through that customer, we ought to stick to some distinctive mark that would hold our manufacturers responsible for turning out the proper article on the one hand and protect our good name on the other. However, I am rather inclined to the view that the idea of the minister is a good one so far as assistance in the expansion of our trade is concerned.

In connection with the
last remark of my hon. friend, I want to say that all other countries, more especially those which are less advanced-[DOT] not speaking slightingly of any country- pay more attention to marks and signs than we do here, and in many cases upon the nature of the sign or the mark depends the decision of the customer as to whether or not he will take the article.
A lesson which we may learn from Japan is that in their large commercial museums 
one of the exhibits consists of articles from almost every country in the world with which the Japanese desire to establish a trade-articles taken right out of the area of use, and just in the form, style and appearance in which they are used and sold. These exhibits are studied by the manufacturers of the cities, the designs are copied and the article, whatever it is, is manufactured and sent out to those countries. I am having my trade commissioners obtain particulars concerning the grades, styles and patterns of various articles in current sale in other countries, and having been brought here so that our manufacturers will see exactly what they are and may copy them if they want to go after the market in those respects.

How much twine do we
export?

I have gone through
orders which have been received by several companies, and the orders are effective provided the Canadian manufacturer will make the article according to instructions; otherwise, they are not. As to how much we really do export, I will get the information for my hon. friend when we come to the Bill. The hon. gentleman must not be too skeptical in the matter; he was very skeptical the other day about my Chinese flour market, but I am going to convince him that there is a better way of looking at these matters.

Perhaps my hon. friend
does not appreciate the point at which I am driving. What I want to find out is: Are we selling twine to any other countries besides Russia, and if so do those other countries demand the same requirements as Russia?
Yes.

I have seen prospective
orders placed, with exactly the same conditions, from the United Kingdom as well as from Russia.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, there has been very little change in connection with the immigration policy which I found on coming into the department. We still pay our bonuses on the classes of immigrants who are admitted under the Act. Domestic servants and agricultural labourers are the classes that are specially encouraged to come to Canada. We impress upon our immigration agents, not only in the old country, but in all countries from which we draw immigration, that no other classes are to be encouraged to come to Canada; in fact, we rather discourage them unless they are coming to assured employment. This is the policy, in the main, that has been enforced for some years and it is being continued under the auspices of myself as Minister of the Interior. During the past year our immigration has increased very materially-I think, in the neighbourhood of 50,000. The immigration for the last fiscal year amounted to 402,000 and of these immigrants there were 150,000 from the British Isles. Immigration from the British Isles has increased very materially, and continental immigration has also increased. The United States immigration fell off somewhat. There may be several reasons for this. The hon. member is aware that the United States press has had very alarming reports about conditions in Canada, and the United States railways, and several states have taken very strenuous efforts to prevent their people emigrating to Canada. Very glaring mis-statements of the condition of affairs in Canada have been published in the United States, press from time to time, and which we have endeavoured to correct, as far as we possibly could. Our agents have reported that while our immigration from the United States has to some extent fallen off, the immigrants we are now receiving, are superior to those we received in past years. As a matter of fact, I think that holds good in regard to immigration from the British Islands and from northern European countries.
1 do not know that there is any particular feature of the immigration policy to which I should make any more particular reference. I have heard my hon. friend refer to the fact that there is not as large a proportion of immigrants going upon the land as he would like to see, and that the homestead entries have fallen off to a con-

sidera/ble extent. It is very true that during the past two or three years there has been a reduction in the homestead entries although there has been a large increase in the applications and issue of patents. During the past fiscal year there were between 32,000 and 33,000 patents issued for homesteads, and during the present fiscal year there have been issued
30.000	patents, which may be increased before the close of the year by another
4.000 or 5,000. There have not been so many homestead entries made, but I would not be at ail surprised if there' is a diminution in the number of homestead entries m the future. Most of the land south of the latitude of Edmonton.-that is land available and in large quantities-has been disposed of in one way or another, either by way of homesteads, preemptions, purchased homesteads, sales to railways, or other methods of disposal
I do not know that it will be the part of wisdom to have a large increase in the number of immigrants going into those northern and more distant parts of the country, or away up in the Peace River country, prior to transportation facilities being provided. In fact, numerous complaints have been addressed to us as well as to the preceding Government, that many of those who have gone in there already have gone in by reason of the literature distributed by the Government representing that particular portion of our country as being a suitable place for immigrants. Some who have gone in there, because of hardships and privations, have had to be grubstaked by the Dominion Government during the winter. Transportation facilities will be afforded in there as time goes on, and naturally the country will fill up but the further you get away from transportation facilities the fewer homestead entries there will be I attribute the falling off in the number of homestead entries to another fact. The various towns and cities in the western part of Canada have had publicity bureaus established and they have been rivalling each other to see whicn city or town could attract the greatest number of immigrants, not only to the city and town itself but to the surrounding country. As a result, many of the .labouring classes, who probably did not intend to go on the land have been attracted to those cities and towns, and as a consequence we have had more unemployment than heretofore. Owing to the fact that the best of our land in the settled districts has been provided with

transportation facilities and owing also to the fact that somewhat strenuous efforts have been made by cities and towns to attract immigrants there have not been so many homestead entries. People do not want to go 100 or 150 miles away from a railway line if they can avoid it.

I have given some consideration to the results of the immigration efforts of the Government of the day, and while I am glad to know that the principles which were followed under the previous Government are still continued by the present Government, it would not, I think, be fair to the country if I did not take the opportunity of pointing out that, according to the records as I read them, the results of the immigration efforts of the present Government have not been as fortunate as those of their predecessors.
I do not wish to be understood as making an essentially unfriendly criticism, but we are here for the purpose of considering matters that . are for the welfare and progress of our country. If it is found that the results achieved under the administration of the Government are not satisfactory, it is the business of the members of the Opposition to call public attention to that
fact.	,
Looking through the returns, and particularly the reports of the Department of the Interior recently issued, I find on comparing the immigration with the occupation of new land, this somewhat startlingly unsatisfactory condition. In the year ending March 31, 1911, we had 311,000 immigrants and 44,479 homestead entries. In the year ending March 31, 1913, we had 402,432 immigrants and 33,699 homestead entries; or in 1913, we had practically 90,000 more immigrants and over 10,000 less homestead entries. When it is considered that the announced policy of this Government as well as of its predecessors, is that the purpose of immigration is to secure the effective and profitable occupation of the vacant lands of the country, it is not necessary further to emphasize the fact, as the record shows that we have been going in the wrong direction. Our increase of immigration in the past two or three years has been an increase of our town population and not an increase of the strength and force, with which we are bringing into productiveness hitherto vacant lands. That fact is emphasized by the reports contained in the Labour Gazette. I have here the Labour Gazette for January, 1914, from which I quote:
The Winnipeg secretary of the Winnipeg' Typographical Union states that the present membership is 483, about 100 of which are at present out of work or working a day a week, and that twenty men have left to seek situations out of Winnipeg.
That is to say, in one of the trades of Winnipeg, more than one-fifth of the total membership is out of employment, and some tradesmen have to leave the city.
Regina: Labour, especially in the building trades, has been unusually quiet, and the number of unemployed is steadily on the increase. December compared unfavourably both with the preceding month and the corresponding, period of last year.
Calgary:	The civic labour bureau haveadopted the plan of employing men by the week for civic work to minimize the hardships of the unemployed as much as possible. The men are employed for a week, then discharged, and another number taken on.
Lethbridge: The close of the year saw conditions exceedingly dull in many lines in Lethbridge. The state of employment was even quieter than during the last month.
Brantford: The condition of the labour market has not improved since last month; if anything, more men are unemployed.
Hamilton: The condition of the labour market during December was more quiet than during the previous month, there being a large number of skilled and unskilled workmen out of employment.
I need not go farther. The conditions-are well known, and it will be generally admitted that we have in our cities at the present time a larger proportion of people out of employment than we have had for many years On the other hand, I find that we have brought 100,000 more people into the country than we did two years ago, and that 10,000 less people have gone on to the land than two years ago. It is evident, therefore, that whatever measures of administration have been pursued by the department in the past, will have to be very seriously revised if the country is to have a return to conditions that prevailed some-years before, when we were receiving a smaller immigration, but having a larger occupation of the land.
About the beginning of last session, as I was informed by the minister, an order was issued by the Immigration Branch relieving immigrants from the necessity of having in their possession $25 between the-lst of April and the last of September, 1913. On the 3rd of May, a month afterwards, it was withdrawn so far as railway and general labourers going into British Columbia were concerned; and it ran until the 6th of June in Tegard to other immigrants.
I thSnk the Government was very well' advised in withdrawing their relaxation of

that regulation, and I commend them very highly for having done so. But a mistake was made, and they by their action admit it, when that order for relaxation was issued. Clearly the department was looking rather to numbers than to quality when they withdrew that twenty-five dollar regulation, and there is no dou'bt that the policy of the department during the preceding year or two was influenced by that idea of numbers rather than quality. The consequence of that policy is that while we have the numbers we have not got the people we want. I quite appreciate the desire of the department to make a record in the matter of numbers of immigrants, but I have always held the view, and I state it here most emphatically, that numbers will not compensate for quality. It is vastly more important that we should have the right kind of people, the people who will meet our needs, and who will find in the country a field adapted to their ability, than to have a great number who are not adapted to the country, and for whom the country is not adapted. My suggestion is-I do not wish to make it in any degree, offensive-that it is because the Government have been guided by the idea of numbers rather than quality that we find ourselves in our present condition for which the Administration is responsible. I am glad they did shut down the lid, but they should never have opened it; they should never have departed from the policy of restriction, selection and direction, which they found in force when they came into office.
There is another point to which I wish to draw attention. There is nothing more terrible in the administration of the Immigration Department than the necessity of enforcing the law as to deportation and rejection at ocean ports. It is hear|| breaking to any man of ordinary sentiment to have to be responsible for what has to be done in order that the welfare of the country be protected:	It is therefore
especially necessary that in every effort that is made to secure immigrants, those who aj;e not desirable should be warned away; that they not only should not be induced to come, but that means be taken at the very source to let them understand they are not wanted in Canada, and th'at they come at the risk of deportation or rejection as the case may be. I am sorry to say that the returns would indicate that the Government have been lax in regard to that matter. Answers given to questions that I have asked, show that in the year 
1910-11 the total number of deportations was 784; in 1911-12, the number was 989; in 1912-13, the number increased to 1,281; and in the first nine months of 1913-14, the latest date for which figures were given me, the deportations numbered 1,503. These people had come into Canada, had been found unsuitable, and had been deported to the countries from which they came.

What is the meaning of
that?

The meaning I draw from that is, that, in the first place, the Government in its administration was not careful to thoroughly inform the immigrating public to whom they were appealing, that this class of people would be deported. I presume there was some slackness at the ocean ports.

Does the hon. member
think this clause of our immigration law should be changed?

No, I am not asking that it be changed, but I am asking for a change in the methods of administration. I am charging, if you like to put it that way, that the Government in their anxiety to secure a large immigration did not cause their . officials to properly inform the immigrating public that if they were found undesirable on coming to Canada they would be deported. Therefore we find that in the first nine months of the current year, we were under the terrible necessity-and it is a terrible necessity in the large majority of cases-of deporting 1,503 of these immigrants. I find no fault with the Government for having deported them. No doubt,, there were eases in which deportation might not be justified, and in all cases there are terrible hardships; but it is the responsibility of i the Government to protect the very life of this country by keeping out undesirable people. The Government was justified, I am assuming, in making the deportations, but the failure was in not having properly warned the people who were in the mind of coming, that if they came and were found to be undesirable they would be deported.
Besides the power of deportation, there is also the responsibility and authority of rejecting immigrants at ocean or boundary ports. As an immigrant comes to the shores of Canada there is a responsibility upon the officials, and authority vested in them, to reject that immigrant under certain fixed conditions. I find that in 1910-11, the last year of the late Government, they rejected

at the ports of Canada, 2,210 persons. These were people who had come to Canada _;and-jyho, having been found unsuitable at the ocean ports, were turned back. Better *do that than allow them to establish themselves here, and finally ha've to send them *out again under the deportation law. In
1911-12, although we had a large increase of immigrants, there were only 972 rejections. It is inconceivable that there should he such a radical difference between the class of immigrants who came in the fiscal year, 1912, and those who came In
1911,	and that more than twice as many -should require to be rejected in 1911 as in
1912.	In the year 1912-13, although there was a still further increase in the number of immigrants, the number of rejections was only 756, but in the nine months of the year 1913-14 thfc rejections were 1,622. That is to say, the Government had discovered their mistake, they had been lax in allowing undesirable people to come in, and in the last nine months they put on the lid and made a number of rejections at the ocean ports corresponding to the number that was made in the last year of the Liberal administration, on a considerably smaller number of immigrants.
I am quite aware that the minister is not personally responsible for all that has taken place since the present Government came into office, [DOT] but he is constitutionally responsible, and he is responsible now for what is to be done in the future. I have desired to show him that the condition is undesirable, and to urge upon him such changes in administration as will carry out effectively, under conditions as they exist, the policy which he himself has declared to-day to be the policy of the Government. Unless we are to have the right kind of people in Canada, we do not want immigrants at all. There is no necessity, however, for assuming that if we adopt a policy of restriction and selection, we will not get immigrants. My view is that if we adopt a proper policy of selection, restriction and direction, together with a proper policy of publicity, we can get, in the present condition of the world, all the immigrants we can properly assimilate, and who from year to year can find a suitable field within our borders. Not only is there no necessity to open the doors wide to let in people who are not fitted for conditions here, but I maintain that by opening the doors wide and Getting in undesirables, to a certain extent we keep out desirable people, thereby injuring the cause for which we are supposed to be working. By being careful in
our selection and definite and strong in our restriction, if we take proper methods of publicity, we can get all the immigration we can usefully employ.
Our immigration from the United States has not shown the increase within this last couple of years that it did in former years, while our immigration from continental Europe does show a very substantial increase. I do not think anybody will question that the immigration that we have hitherto received from the United States, being largely composed of farmers-men who have sold their land in the States and come to Canada fully equipped for the occupation of our new land, or men who have been in farming employment there, and who also come well equipped

are essentially desirable. But that immigration has fallen off within recent months, while the immigration from continental Europe of people whose intent is to enter upon city life rather than the improvement of the soil has increased. To my mind there is a relation between the two conditions, and in proportion as you flood your country with immigrants whose activities you do not desire, to that extent you render the country less attractive to the people whose activities you do desire. On that point, let me give the House the figures. In 1911 we had 123,013 British immigrants, 121,451 United States immigrants, and 66,000 others. In 1913 we had 150,542 British, 139,009 United States, and 112,881 immigrants from other countries. In two years the increase from continental Europe was greater than the united increase from the United States and Great Britain. I must insist that that is not a satisfactory condition. It does not show that the .activities of the department were properly directed, and I bring the matter to the attention of the minister for the purpose of urging on him that in the administration of his department he will so direct his activities as to increase the immigration of those who are best suited to our country and to whom our country is best suited, so that their places shall not be occupied by people who are less suited to the country and to whom the country is less suited.
Mr. PA.QUET: The hon. gentleman was at one time Minister of the Interior; can he give the committee any information as to the best way to remedy the condition with regard to immigration coming from the United States?

I do not know that I have any suggestion to offer at the moment. I

am dealing with the subject of restricting immigration rather than of encouraging it. My argument to-day is that we have not had the restriction which we should have had, and contrariwise and as a consequence of that in a measure, we have not had the flow of immigration to the sections that we desire. I have no doubt that the minister is using due endeavours to secure people from the United States. I was not urging him to use greater endeavours in that particular at the moment, for we can take that up at some other time. I was urging him to use restrictive measures against people who are less desirable and who are occupying the country to the country's detriment and to the detriment of the desirable immigrant, whether he comes from the United States or from any other country.
I wish to point out that there is no question about the number of people in the United States available to be induced to come to Canada as the record of past years has shown. It is a mere matter of the publicity given to the advantages of Canada. I have no doubt that the present conditions in the agricultural industry in western Canada do not offer that inducement to immigration from the United States that they would under other circumstances. I do not wish to bring that question into this argument, but I wish to draw attention to the fact that, we have not by any means exhausted the British field. I find from the last report of the United States Commissioner General of Immigration that the United States secured last year from England 43,363 immigrants, from Ireland, 27,876, from Scotland, 14,220, and from Wales 2,745. To these very people do we look for the filling up of this country, and the perpetuation of'our social and governmental conditions, and yet we find that in the last year over 75,000 of them went to the United States. If other people are able to secure immigrants from these British Isles so should we, and it is only a matter of the system of publicity that is followed by the department and of advantageous conditions here. It appears to me that the department has been following a policy of numbers rather than of quality in their immigration propaganda both in the British Islands and on the continent of Europe. In the interests of Canada I would urge very strongly that they change not the law, but their policy under the law.
I wish further to allude to a matter that has been up for consideration

in this, House on several occasions *and is sufficiently important to warrant the attention of the minister. The report of the Commissioner General of Immigration of the United States for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1912, deals at considerable length with the question of emigration from the United States to Canada and of immigration from Canada to the United States, and the -figures given in the report are certainly remarkable. The matter was brought to my attention when I was minister by the present Prime Minister; and I am bound to say that I did not tnen give it that attention it possibly merited. However, the circumstances being as they are, the Government should take notice of the conditions. The present Prime Minister urged very strongly that the matter should be considered" thoroughly by the Government, and now that he has control of the affairs of the country, of course we would naturally expect that he would take the course he then laid down for us. In the year 1911, this report states, the movement of population from -Canada to the United States was 105,512, while the movement from the United States to Canada was 119,753; and that in 1911-12 the movement from the United -States to Canada was 143,251, and the movement from Canada to the United States 107,953.
Does the hon. gentleman think that those statistics are correct?

I would hesitate to challenge an official statement such as this, but I must -say that it does not impress me as being correct. However, it is a -statement that has been given wide publicity and I would suggest to the minister that possibly the department has information in Tegard to this matter, and that it would be well that he should give to the House such information as he has upon the subject. If we take the figures as authentic, it certainly puts us in a very unfortunate position so far as immigration bom the United States is concerned. I would think from my own observation that the figures given cannot be correct. I think the minister should inform the House and the country as to how far those figures are correct and give what information he lias in regard to the matter.

Has the Department of
the Interior any system whatever of inspection, medical or otherwise, at the ports of debarkation?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I understand that immigrants coming from foreign ports have to

submit in their own country to an examination much the same as that held by the Board of Trade in Great Britain, where- they are examined by the steamship companies, and by the British Board of Trade doctors.
Are they examined when they land here?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Certainly.

Has the Government a
medical inspector at Portland, Maine?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

But the department has
no regular inspector in foreign ports. My hon. friend from I/Islet (Mr. Paquet) is my authority for the statement that the Americans have a strict medical inspection of immigrants destined for the United States at the port of embarkation. That is very important because there is nothing more painful than the deportation of an immigrant as every one will admit. A deported immigrant when he gets back to his own country produces a very sorrowful impression upon his neighbours. The deportation of one immigrant, perhaps deservedly deported, may mean the loss to Canada of ten or fifteen most desirable citizens. A system of medical inspection in foreign countries, of immigrants destined for Canada would be of great benefit. It would not require a very large outlay of money as compared with the immense amount we are spending on immigration, and I urge the department to consider this matter and to introduce legislation if necessary. In view of the number of unemployed in this country, we should keep closer watch than ever on our immigration. A few days ago I was travelling from Montreal to an American town and I noticed the American immigration inspector making a most thoi-ough examination of all the passengers on the train. Three travellers who, in my opinion, had a very attractive appearance were deported at St. Albans by the inspector. He was not a medical officer but that incident shows, I think, that the American system of inspection is much more severe than ours.
I understand that these three travellers, who were Canadians, were turned back because they stated they had secured employment in some American city. If we had a system of medical inspection in foreign countries, it would prevent the sailing of many people who think they may escape inspection on this side of the ocean, and encourage wholesome immigration. I hope the minister will take this suggestion of mine
in good part and that legislation to this effect will be introduced, if he finds it advisable.

My hon. friend has referred to the unemployed. The minister must, I am sure, have received a circular which was sent to him and many other members explaining why there are so many unemployed in this country at the present time. Without commenting on it, I wish to put that circular on ' Hansard.' The steamship companies are inducing men to come here by promising them all kinds cf good things. Nobody will class me as a partisan for saying that, as I said the same thing when the Liberals were in power, and I have voted against them time and again on that question as the record shows.
I do not say that the Government are responsible for it, but they should prevent these companies from doing such things, if they are receiving so much per head for bringing immigrants into this country. Men are men and companies are composed of men, and the almighty dollar is just as good to them as to anybody else. If they are bonused for anything of that kind, and I am not saying they are, it should be stopped. The circular to which I have referred reads in part:
The General Agency-The Transatlantic in London, England, has been commissioned to place 1,500 men in the following works: The Dominion Steel Corporation and Dominion Coal Company, Limited, in Glace Bay, and the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, Limited, in Sydney, Canada.
The following men are required. Miners (cutters)-possessing certificates. Payments by the ton. Cutters earn from 60 to 100 roubles a fortnight (1 rouble equals 51 p.c.). Assistant cutters-payment by the ton, an average wage of 4 roubles a day and even more. Unskilled workers-(1,000 to 1,500) for work above and below ground. Wages, between 14 and 15 cents per hour. Nobody is bound to work underground but the better wages are paid for this work.
Coke oven workers for Sydney-wages about 15 cents per hour. Work time 11 hours but work is light. Foundry workers for Sydney- work 10 hours. Wages the same as coke oven workers.
Workers for stone quarrying-in Marble Mountain. Work time 10 hours. Wages about 15 cents per hour. Life in the Marble Mountain is very pleasant.
No experience and no knowledge is demanded. Every healthy and willing man will be engaged. The following are also required. Stokers-4 roubles a day. Iron turners, carpenters, and foundryworkers and others.
Every unskilled worker who is in communication with the general agency, the Transatlantic, may be sure of employment the first day of arrival. A minimum wage of 2.8 roubles (Jl-43) will be guaranteed to begin immediately. Later 4 roubles a day can be earned. Skilled

workers can earn 4.8 roubles a day (about $2.80).
The works management looks after board and lodging. The necessary outlay amounts to 80 kopecks (approximately 40 cents a day), so that each worker can save out of his own wages 2 roubles a day (about $1.03). In cases of sickness the workers receive medical attendance and financial assistance to the extent of 10 roubles a week. The travelling expenses must be borne by the workers themselves. No money will be advanced by the works management. Knowledge of the language is not necessary. In Canada, and especially in the trades in question, there are many Russians and many workers from Austria and the Balkan States, so that every worker can get along with his mother tongue.
Every worker who wishes to emigrate to Canada should write to the office of the general agency, stating his name, age, nationality, and the name of the ship in which he will sail, and the date of the sailing to Canada. He will then receive a certificate of employment gratis from this office. Whoever possesses a certificate will experience no difficulty in landing in Canada.
The circular says that there is no trouble in landing in Canada, but I hope that the immigration law will not allow immigrants to land here unless they have the amount of money they are supposed to have. 1 read another article on this very subject to-day, published in the British Columbia Federationist, a labour paper, under date of March 6 of this year. We find that Mackenzie and Mann, who have a kind of immigration line themselves, also send circulars of the same character throughout Europe. They are anxious to get men to work in their mines iin British Columbia and on their railways throughout Canada. This sort of propaganda is being carried on notwithstanding the fact that we know that there are a lot of men idle. If the company that issued this circular say that we are in need of skilled mechanics they are the worst liars that I ever met in my life, because every day almost it becomes more and more apparent that we do not need any skilled mechanics and there is a surplus of other labour in the country at the present time. I would call upon the Government to see if they cannot prevent others from coming in. If it was proper for the Government to pass an Order in Council to prevent immigration going into British Columbia for a certain period, which wall soon expire, then similar legislation should be passed with reference to other parts of the country when there are so many idle people with a poor prospect of getting work even when the spring opens.
I may be told that railway construction and operation will start again in the 
sprang. Railway construction and operation will not give employment to all the idle men in the country at the present time, and with the present financial situation it is doubtful if the resumption of building operations will provide work for all the -skilled mechanics who are at present unemployed. That is one reason why we should be very careful about doing anything which will encourage men to flock to the cities as they have done in the past. I read in the House some years ago a statement with reference to the manner in which men are brought to this country. I visited a portion of Europe in 1910, I went into different immigration offices and I saw a great many men whs were preparing to come to this country. While 1 would not under any consideration ask them not to come, I am convinced that there is a great deal of misrepresentation, as is evidenced in this circular here in which it is -said that from 1,000 to 1,500 men are wanted, a statement which is absolutely incorrect. This circular which I have read was reprinted from the Daily Province, of Vancouver, of January 7, 1914. The Government should do all in their power to prevent any similar action being taken by any other company. The other night I saw a statement in the Federationist, and if my hon. friend the minister will look at that paper he will see that the guilty party i-s one who used to be in the employ of the Salvation Army and who has done a great deal of harm bringing immigration to this country by misrepresentation. These letters and circulars originate in Toronto and they are sent broadcast in the old country and in Europe in order to induce immigrants to come to British Columbia and other parts of Canada, a propaganda which is absolutely unfair.

I would like to call
the minister's attention to the fact that an anomaly exists in connection with the duties of some of the immigration agents who are paid so much per head for distributing the immigrants who are brought into the country. It frequently happens that these men, for -some reason or other, do not stay in the situations in which they are placed. Other people come to the Government immigration agent knowing that he has to do with immigrants and employment, and they say:	'We will take those
men,' or ' We will take men.' It so Imp-pens that the Government immigration agent is precluded from taking a fee from

those men for placing them in positions. The consequence is that, as they get their income in that way, if they place them there, they are cutting themselves off from their income. The net result is that either they must forego the simplest duty of their office and refuse to place these men in positions that are waiting for them, in order that they may place men who are brought out from the old country in the spring in those positions, and that they may get their pay per head, or else, they must place them and assist in settling the difficulties of the employment problem' in the country without receiving any pay for doing so. That really is a hardship that ought to be remedied. In Peterborough, we have a very fine Government immigration agent in Mr. Miller, who has time and again placed men who have not been able to stay in the positions which he has found for them, after remaining there from one, two, three or six months. They may have left either owing to the fault of the position or of themselves, but Mr. Miller says: ' I cannot see these fellows going around idle when I know of places where I can place them.' Therefore he places men in those positions, but he gets nothing for it; and in that way, when immigrants-come out in the spring, he may have no places for them, so that he is between the devil and the deep sea. There ought to be some solution of this problem, although I do not know what it is.
Whether it is a problem for the Minister of the Interior or for the Minister of Labour, I cannot say; but the balance between supply and demand should certainly receive a greater degree of superintendence. It frequently happens that in different centres of the country there are more men than are necessary for the work, and still they keep coming in. What are we to do? They have either to be taken care of by the municipality or become burdens of a worse class on the community. At the present time, so far as I know or can find out, this superintendence is not exercised at all. The great cry is: Bring on your immigrants; fetch them in; fill up the country, so that we can say that the statistics show that the population is rapidly increasing. Population increasing in that irregular way is simply an absurdity. If in trade, supply and demand maintain more or less of a balance and adjustment, there ought to be something of an automatic character with regard to men; but, strange to say, in the whole theory of public employment,
the man, that is to say the life of the individual, is given no consideration at all. The whole thing is treated on a basis of trade, of goods, of bargain and sale. Until we have reformed this, and remember that the life of the men, women and children of the country is the first consideration, we shall never have reached even the primary Stages of civilization.

A few days ago I, asked the following questions of the Department of the Interior:
1.	Has the Government rented an office to be used by the immigration agent at Edmunds-ton, N.B.?
2.	If so, why is said office not occupied?
3.	How much rent was paid to the lessor till the 31st of December last?
The answers were:
1.	Yes.
2.	Department understands office is used for purposes for which it is rented.
3.	$100, at the rate of $10 per month, heat, light and telephone included.
This office has not been occupied for one hour since it has been rented, and yet the Government has been paying ten dollars a month for over a year. I draw the attention of the minister to this fact,, because I do not think that he is aware of what is going on in my constituency. The office is owned by a Mr. Boudreau, a barber, who is a good friend of the gentleman in charge of the patronage in my constituency. The inspector of the Immigration Department was in Edmundston before this office was rented, and he went around the town and picked out a decent office for our immigration agent. He had almost completed the arrangement when it was found out that this good office belonged to a Liberal, and consequently the latter gentleman could not get any money from this Government. Therefore the gentleman who has charge of the patronage-
What is his name?

Mr. Cormier, my last
opponent. Mr. Cormier met the immigration agent and made him change his mind, and the inspector had to call upon Mr. Boudreau, the barber, and rent the office which is located behind the barber shop. You have to walk through the barber shop in order to reach this little office, which is about six feet square.
Amongst the razors.

Is the barber shop six
feet square?

No. The office rented
for the immigration agent. A large number of the people who call on the immigration agent are priests and professional men. Sometimes one of our priests, who has difficulties in connection with certain immigrants coming from the state of Maine to our country, has to visit the immigration agent, and he would have to walk through the barber shop to arrive at the office of the immigration agent. I suppose the first question the barber would ask the priest would be:	'Do you want a shave or a
hair cut? ' More than that, I am informed *that the immigration agent at Edmundston has refused to occupy that office, because he tells me that alongside of it there is a water closet, and the partition between the hall and the water closet is only half way up to the ceiling, so that there is an open space for an atmosphere to spread not only along the hall but pretty close to this office. I know, of course, that the hon. minister is not aware of all these facts; but I ask him that he stop payment at once, because I think that our barber is making a good business out of his shop and is not entitled to an annual rent of $120. The Government have been very kind to their friends, but I do not think they would care to go so far if they were aware of what is going on. In the upper part of New Brunswick, the gentlemen who are handling the patronage are not always looking after the interest of their party or of the Government. I desire, [DOT]therefore, to ask the minister not to tolerate this monthly rent of $10 any longer.
What is the name of the paper you have just quoted?

It is La Justice, published at Ottawa. That Mr. Baulby is head immigration and repatriation officer for the New England States, where the people to be repatriated are largely French Canadians, notwithstanding which that officer does not speak a single work of French.
How is it that for the purpose of repatriating people who for the most part are French Canadians, men are appointed who are unable to understand them, who do not speak a single word of the language spoken by those with whom they are supposed to be in daily intercourse? For that state of things, this Government should not be held responsible; we found things in that very situation when we came into power. Unfortunately it may fairly be urged against us that we have done very little toward bringing about a change, and Mr. Baulby'3 case is not the only one of its kind in the New England States.
But that is not the whole story. While we are thus spending large sums in the interest of immigration, we are apparently, on the other hand, doing all in our power to prevent any results accruing from our efforts, and our own agents are not alone in taking that stand in complete opposition with the country's public interest, Let me quote certain facts in support- of my contention.
For some years past, we have had on all our railway lines connecting with the United States immigration inspectors. Last year, I applied to the House for a list of the inspectors who were on duty over the railways operating in the province of Quebec, and the_information supplied was that immigration inspectors number altogether eighteen, viz.: six English-speaking, eleven French-speaking, and one Italian. So then, out of a total of 18 men doing service in the province of Quebec, where nine tenths of the immigrants entering Canada from the United States are French Canadians re-

turning home, there are, as will be seen, seven men who do not speak a word of French, while the 11 French Canadians fluently speak both languages. Now, according to my contention, those eighteen inspectors should be able to fluently speak both languages.
To show you how inefficient are those who do not speak the French language, and under what difficulties they must labour at times in the performance of their duties, I once put to one of them the following question: What Government are you working for, the United States or the Canadian Government? He was unable to answer that simple question, a proof that he was utterly ignorant of the French language. On another occasion, I put to an immigration agent, or rather immigration inspector, by the name of Stahl, the following question, three times in succession: What is your name? Surely a very simple question, and he never understood- or let on that he did. Can it be supposed for a single moment that such men have the necessary qualifications and the necessary knowledge to gather information, form opinions or enquire about French Canadians, several of whom do not speak English?
Would this Government keep for a single day along the United States boundary a man who did not speak English? How then under such conditions can these men properly fulfil the duties incumbent on them?
Our fellow-countrymen, while crossing the line, are oftentimes subjected to a good deal of unnecessary hardship, and they may esteem themselves fortunate if those allpowerful office holders do not shut them off entirely from Canada. What is the use of spending thousands of dollars in an effort to repatriate our people, when we have at the boundary government officers who impede our efforts and even defeat them in 'some cases.
I have just mentioned the name of Stahl. I happened to be once on the same train, and an incident occurred under my eyes concerning which I would like to have some explanations from the hon Minister of the Interior.
I would like now to ask the hon. minister a question, and in order that he may understand it well, I wish to read an extract from certain correspondence I had with the department with regard to the refusal of an immigration inspector tp allow a certain lady to enter into Canada from the United States. When I reported the case to the minister he communicated with his officer and asked him for an explanation. In the

letter written, by Mr. Scott with regard to the matter, I find this paragraph:
Eva Boucher was a passenger in the first class coach, she was of good appearance and neatly dressed, travelling by herself, and had a ticket from Berlin, N.H., to Montreal. Her parents were French Canadians, but she herself was born at Lewiston, Me., and is now twenty years old and not married. Her father and mother have not been living together for the past two years. Her father is at Kamouraska, P.Q., and her mother at Lewiston, Me.
What I want to know is whether under these circumstances the immigration inspector had the right to put that girl off the train.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If she had not conformed with the Canadian immigration laws, most assuredly the inspector was justified in doing so. I understand she did not conform with the laws.
In what respect?	.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
not told the whole story. This girl was an undesirable born in the United States, and, being a United States citizen, she had to conform with our immigration laws. There was another reason for her rejection not disclosed here, and which I do not care to mention.
In what way did she fail to conform with the immigration law-s? Her parents were born in Canada, she was under twenty-one years of age and had a ticket to Montreal.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My understanding of the
law is that a ticket to Montreal or any other point of destination in Canada will not permit any person bom in the United States to come into this country under conditions which contravene our immigration laws.
Does the minister affirm that a persofi who is under twenty-one yeaAs of age and whose parents were born in Canada, is not a Canadian?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, I affirm that that girl, born in the United States of French-Can-adian parents, is a United States citizen.

On what article of the
law does the minister base that opinion? I find in the Revised Statutes of 1906, volume 2, chapter 93, page 67, a definition of what is a British subject and what is a Canadian subject. I find that so long as a person is not a United States subject and is under twenty-one years of age, he is, if 103J
born of Canadian parents, a Canadian. I am not a lawyer, of course, but under this law I do not see any reason why the inspector should shut the door of this country to any person under these circumstances. This girl could not choose to be a citizen of the United States until after she was twenty-one years old. If there has been any ' change in the law, I would like to know of it.
Is the mother of that girl a citizen of the United States?

No; from the conversation I had with the girl on the train, I understood that her father and mother were both French-Canadians, born in this country. I would like to be well posted in regard to this matter, because such cases may occur in the future.

I think my hon. friend is right. If that girl was born of French-Canadian parents who were born in this country, until she attained the age of twenty-one she would be of the nationality of her parents.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: She was born in the United States.
Even so, if her parents were horn in Canada she would follow the nationality of her parents until she could choose for herself.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Would not something
depend upon whether or not her father had become naturalized in the United States?

Possibly, but the assertion made by the hon. member for Rimouski is that the girl was born ot
British subjects residing at the time in the United States. Legally*, she was under age, therefore her nationality was that of her parents. Her parents being British subjects, she was a British subject also, unless, being twenty-one years of age, she chose to become a citizen of the United States. I think my hon. friend's contention is strong, that until this girl attained the age of twenty-one years, she would follow the nationality of her parents.
Mr. BOULAY': I reported this case to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, and asked him for an investigation, which was refused. At the time, I asked the inspector to give me his name, as well as the reason why he was putting the girl off the train. I tried to speak to him in a gentlemanly way and to make him under-
<624

stand that I thought he was not complying with the law, but he was impolite enough not to listen to me, and even threatened "to have me arrested if I continued to *question him in any way. In his letter, the travelling inspector said:
It Mr. Boulay had informed Mr. Stahl who he was and had asked him on what ground this girl was being refused, Mr. Stahl states he would have given Mr. Boulay the information, but as he did not know Mr. Boulay and took him to be one of the passengers who had no right to interfere with him, he felt it his duty to let him know that he had instructions to carry out with reference to such cases without giving any information to any passenger who might come along.
This is not the truth at all. He would not even give me the opportunity to tell him who I was although I tried to do it, because I did not want to interfere in any way with the exercise of his functions. All I wanted to know was the ground on which he was rejecting her because from the explanation given to me I was sure that the girl was a Canadian citizen and had a right to come to this country without being molested by a Government officer.

I would like to emphasize what the hon. member (Mr. Boulay) has said regarding the immigration inspectors on the international trams between the United States and Canada. A good many of those inspectors cannot speak the French language, and this matter was brought to the attention of the Minister of Public Works last year. I would not say, as my hon. friend from Rimouski his said, that the large majority of the passengers on the trains from the United States speak French, but I fancy he meant the repatriated Canadians. I understand that the majority of the passengers as a rule are English speaking, but quite a proportion of them are of French origin and do not understand English at all, and many of those officers who cannot speak French are in consequence unable to perform the duties of their position. The inspection, therefore, is quite inefficient in many cases and I would urge upon the minister to see that, whatever his nationality, every inspector should speak both languages, because he is liable to meet people who do not speak in any other language but French.

I have here an editorial taken from the Toronto Globe of January 26, 1914, in which reference is made to an article in the London Times regarding a convict who was allowed to go with twelve months in jail on the promise that he would

come to Canada afterwards. The name and other particulars are given. Perhaps the minister could briefly tell -what action has been taken by his department to prevent such action by magistrates and other authorities in the old country, because apparently this is not the only instance in which criminals have been given consideration if they would come to Canada.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No matter of that kind has ever been brought to my personal attention. 1 am aware that in years gone by the newspapers reported cases in which magistrates in the old country had allowed criminals to go on the promise that they would emigrate to some of the colonies; but I thought that was rather out of date now. I do not think that practice now prevails. This may be an isolated case. Of course, there is no justification, for it, and the only way we can get back is to let some of our criminals go on condition that they will move over to England.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In all those laws there has to be exercised common sense on the part of the officials. I do not think that any officer, knowing his duty, would reject a member of a family, if the father or mother were already in Canada, by reason of one member of the family having lost an eye, or being lame or something of that kind. In a case of tubercular trouble, for example, we would not allow them into the country, not only owing to the danger of infection, but because they might marry and have diseased children. In cases such as those referred to by the hon. member for Brantford, it is not necessary to change our laws. I think our officers do exercise discretion, and they are experienced men who have these cases coming up every day. I feel quite sure that they would not reject any person under such circumstances, because of some minor defect.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Would the minister refer to the matter of inter-migration between Canada and the United States, about which I was speaking before 6 o'clock ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Edmonton has pointed out that the immigration from the United States is larger than formerly, but that fewer immigrants are going on the land. I have already given the reasons so that it will not be necessary for me to go over them again. The hon. member seemed to blame the Government to a certain extent for the falling off in our immigration from the United States and for the large number of continental immigrants coming in.. He stated that we were getting numbers but not quality, and that this continental immigration was the cause of the falling off m our immigration from the United States.
It is true there have not been so many homestead entries during the past two years as heretofore, and I should not be at all surprised if we have reached the maximum number of homestead entries for any one year, at all events until we can get better transportation facilities into that portion of our country where a large area of homestead lands still exist. We must not forget, however, that according to the reports I have from the officers, a great many
of the American immigrants of last year brought considerably more cash than those coming in previous years. Having money, these immigrants have not taken up free lands but have purchased farms from the Government, or from companies or individuals and have located nearer to the towns and cities. That accounts to a considerable extent for the falling off in homestead entries. Other factors have been the propaganda carried on in the United States, misrepresentations in the United States * press, as well as the fact, which .1 did not touch on before, that recently liberal concessions have been made to homesteaders in the United States. They are now offering in the state of Montana! what are known as enlarged homesteads, consisting of 320 acres of land, instead of 160 acres as formerly, and the homesteader can get his patent in three years instead of five. This tends to keep some of the- people at home. They have adopted the regulation: That the homesteader has to be m residence on his land ' seven months in each of the three years, instead of six as formerly, and this provision is intended to do away with what is known as the professional homesteader. Our regulations compel a homesteader to reside six months on his land in each of the three years, before getting his patent, and it is to prevent a man qualifying in Canada for a homestead and then going across to the United States and qualifying there that the seven months' residence has been insisted on.
The hon. member for Edmonton has referred to certain statistics in regard to our American immigrants who return to the United States and I was very glad to hear the hon. member state that he did not believe the American, figures were correct. I am quite convinced they are not. Their system of counting immigrants is different from ours. When a homeseeker comes to-the Canadian Northwest from the United States and spends two or three moitths in our country he is not counted by our agent's as an immigrant. When he returns to the United States after spending a few months in Canada looking for a home he is considered by the American authorities as a . returned immigrant. It can easily be seen, how that would swell the figures of returned immigrants to the United States. We-have followed up this n.-estion very closely and I have a memorandum on the subject, extracts of which I shall read:
On account of the head tax charged by the United States upon immigrants entering that country, the tendency is to class as immigrants many who have not really decided to reside-

in the United States but may be going there for a visit only. Similarly, regarding United States citizens, the United States officials count as returning to the States to settle many who have never been included in Canadian immigration statistics but who have been merely in Canada to look over opportunities for investment, etc.
The department secured some time ago from the United States officials a list of the names of the parties who were reported as having gone to the United States in November, 1910, and w'ho in their statistics were classed as Canadians settling in the States. A large number of these people were interviewed by Officers of this department, and out of a total of S49 who were classed in the United States returns as going to settle in that country 416 were found to have gone on a visit only or for merely temporary employment and had at the time of the investigation already returned to Canada. A similar investigation was made of Canadian citizens reported in United States statistics to have gone to the United States in August, 1912, to settle there, the result of which investigation was to show that 50 per cent who were classed as settlers for the United States had already returned to the Dominion.
In the comparison of various sets of statistics it is absolutely necessary that due regard should be given to the basis upon which they are prepared. In this connection I would call your special attention to the different standards existing in the preparation of Canadian immigration and United States immigration statistics. In Canada a new arrival is counted as an immigrant only upon his first arrival in the country, and if he returns year after year to his native land and at a later date comes back to Canada, he is on the second and each succeeding return classed for statistical purposes as a returned Canadian or non-immigrant irrespective of the length of time which he may have lived in the Dominion. In the United States statistics, on the other hand, persons other than United States citizens are classed as immigrants upon each arrival. It is well known that many Canadians yearly spend the winter in the lumber camps of Maine and Michigan, while at all times it is common for families in the eastern provinces to go to the eastern States for periods o( varied lengths to secure employment in the cotton mills or other manufacturing industries there without intending to permanently settle in the republic. If a lumberman of Quebec were to go each year for 10 years to work in the woods of Maine, he would be classed in the Uhited States statistics for that decade as 10 immigrants; and from this explanation it is clearly apparent that many Canadians are counted as immigrants to the United States who in reality go there for a temporary purpose only, and that year afteiv year, at least in some cases, the same persons are counted twice or oftener as settling in the United States. This system results in an apparent loss to Canada which in reality does not exist, at least to the extent which the United States immigration figures would lead one to believe.
Of the United States immigration to Canada only about 60 per cent, according to Canadian statistics, were born in the United States, and yet we find, according to the censuses of 1901 and 1911, that the United States born in Canada has increased from 127,899 to 303,6S0. On the other hand, United States statistics
IMr. Roche.]
which are quoted to create the impression of a large movement from Canada to the United States claim that this alleged movement contains 43 per cent Canadian citizens, but when we turn to the United States censuses of 1900 and 1910 we find that during that decade the Canadian born residents of the republic have increased from 1,179,807 to only 1,204,637, or a total increase of 24,830, certainly a small number upon to base a story of any immense movement of population.
And so I might go on to the same effect, but what I have read is sufficient to show that the method of compiling statistics in the United States differs very materially from that in Canada, that you get no correct grasp of the movement of population from those statictics, and that they are not compiled in anything like as correct a manner as are our Canadian statistics.
My hon. friend from Edmonton has spoken about quality being overlooked in our efforts to get numbers into the country. I am quite ready to agree, as I am sure my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland), a brother medical man, is, that there is nothing to be gained by allowing great numbers to come into the country if it is going to be at the expense of the quality of our population. I am sure we are all sincerely desirous of seeing the standard of our citizenship maintained. I personally would not grieve to see our immigration diminished considerably in numbers,- if as a result, we were to get superior quality. - Everything has impressed itself on my mind to the effect that we are getting superior quality. Our own officers say so, the United States officers admit it, and our officers in England say so. We have had the same officials here in charge of our immigration movement as those who were in charge when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, these gentlemen have had experience of the immigration propaganda and the way it should be conducted and they are not, by reason of a change of minister, or a change of government, going to fall so far short in the discharge of their duties as to bring about the dire results which my hon. friend from Edmonton would make us believe, have been brought about in the administration of the Immigration Act. There has been no violent change in connection with the administration of that Act.
Another thing which the hon. gentleman pointed to was that we had relaxed, for a short period during the early portion of last season, the money qualification. Surely, that would not make so great a difference and if it is to be laid as a fault at our door

well, we have had valu-

able precedents. We did so by reason of the fact that, owing to the Balkan war which had been going on, and draining our country of thousands and thousands of the labourers and navvies who are accustomed to work on our railways, the railway companies made representations to the Government that there was apt to be a scar-' city of railway labour in Canada last season. It had occurred during the preceding season. They said that they had been considerably handicapped by reason of not securing a sufficient supply of labourers, and it was urged that the money qualifica-'. tion stood in the way. This is not a new departure. Every year since 1908, for a greater or lesser period, there has been a relaxation of the money qualification. Owing to representations made to us the relaxation of the money qualification existed for little more than a month, but as soon as it w'as seen that we were going to have an abundance of labour for the season, the qualification of $25 for the summer months was restored. I do not think any grave violence was done to the interests of the country by reason of the relaxation. But we have sent a circular to each of our agents, to each steamship company, and to each port agent, which reads:
Sir,-As you are aware, the department has on some occasions relaxed the money qualification and other regulations when it was clearly apparent that sufficient immigrants could not be secured without such action. This year it is anticipated that there will be sufficient arrivals of immigrants fully complying with monetary and other regulations, and consequently it has been definitely decided during 1914 no relaxation of regulations will be made for labourers, skilled or unskilled, whether going to assured employment or not. The extra privileges conferred upon farmers, farm labourers and female domestic servants under P.C. 924 will be continued as in the past.
The department trusts that you will make every effort to have all your agents thoroughly familiar with the attitude of the department so that there will be no necessity for rejecting upon arrival persons seeking entry into Canada.
This circular was sent out on the 10th February of this year in order to forestall any influx of immigrants not belonging to the bonused, or the domestic servant, or agricultural labouring classes. We have taken every precaution to discourage immigrants coming to Canada, even although they come upon their own responsibility, unless they are able to pass the medical examination and money qualification as well.
My hon. friend from Edmonton has stated that the immigration from southern Europe has increased and is still increasing in very large proportion. The Government are not doing anything to encourage those immigrants coming to the country. The fact is that those people have been preceded by their fellow-countrymen who came out under the auspices of the preceding Government, and they, having made good, are sending back money for relatives and friends and are encouraging them to come to Canada. We are not paying any bonus for these people. How are we to exclude them unless we pass a prohibitory Act entirely, if they are able to pass the monetary qualification and the medical examination?
