Under these circumstances, I do not think that we can be blamed for this large number of southern European immigrants.
The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) has touched upon a point regarding the medical examination of immigrants coming to Canada from foreign countries.
I realize, as he does, how important it is to have a rigid medical examination, but I would draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that if we were to attempt the policy of having our own medical examiners in a great many of those foreign countries we would find it impracticable. We could hot enforce such examination, because most of those countries prevent us from carrying on an immigration propaganda of any kind within their borders.
If we are not allowed to induce immigration by any m earns from those countries,
[DOT] we would surely not be allowed to have medical examiners there. Many of those countries have examinations by their own medical examiners similar to those exacted by the British Board of Trade. And in addition to that we have our own medical examination in Canada which is much stricter than that exacted by the British Board of Trade. I am desirous of seeing that examination conducted in the most rigid manner. If you saw .some of the correspondence I am in receipt of protesting against the medical examination, such as the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-sbutt) spoke of before .six o'clock, you would find that we are charged with being far too rigid in our exactions so far as the medical examination is concerned. On the boundary our examination is much the same as that of the United States. They have quite a rigid medical examination; but still last year on our boundary inspectors' examinations, we rejected upwards of 17,000. That speaks volumes in favour of the manner in which our medical examination is conducted.
That is from the United States?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Either coming through
United States ports or from the United States. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) compared the number of deportations and rejections with the number cf immigrants coming to Canada, but the more rejections we have the better it speaks for the examination. In 1907-08, when there came to this country 120,182 immigrants, there were deported 825; whereas the very next year, 1908-09, the number of immigrants coming to Canada fell from 120,182 to 52,000, but the deportations numbered 1,748 so that with less than half the number of immigrants, the deportation more than doubled. This is exactly on a parity with the illustration which my hon. friend gave. While our medical examination may be improved and I hope to see it improved from time to time, I think if is even now a very rigid examination. With more immigrants coming to the country, necessarily there will be more deportations. The Government has not been to blame for this. The steamship companies probably are in very many instances to blame, perhaps by not being circumspect enough and allowing many undesirable immigrants to board the boats at the point of embarkation. We threatened the steamship companies with legal proceedings unless they exercise greater precaution, and they have been doing so. By keeping them* up to the scratch, I have no doubt that we shall have a material improvement.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) referred to a circular that is being sent out by certain companies to induce immigrants to come to uur country, and which states that certain certificates will be furnished them upon presentation of which at the Canadian ports of entry they will be permitted to enter Canada without the necessary medical qualification. I have not seen that circular before; it has never been brought to our attention. I can assure my hon. friend that those companies have absolutely no justification whatever and no authority from this Government for such conduct. The people they may bring into this country, if they bring any, must conform with the monetary regulations. The Government are not assisting that class of immigrants by way of bonuses to come to Canada. It must be a misrepresentation on the part of any society or company who are endeavouring to bring these people to Canada on the ground that there is plenty

of employment and that the immigration regulations will be waived in their behalf.
The hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) referred to the fact that certain of our commission immigration agents who receive two dollars a head for placing immigrants with farmers, are denied the privi-* lege of exacting a similar fee on those whom they could find in other employments. It was not the policy of the department under the preceding Government, or under this, to.pay a commission to any of those agents for securing employment for immigrants except in agricultural work. Otherwise we would be converting our staff into employment agencies. There are employment bureaus, for which we have appointed inspectors, whose duty it is to protect the immigrants from undue exactions. We are not, however, turning our agents into employment bureaus to find employment in the various industrial walks of life for immigrants coming to our shores.	.
The hon. gentleman also thought that it would be quite proper for us to allow these immigration agents to be paid two dollars a head to secure employment for those who are not immigrants. Our immigration agents are not expected to do that. They are paid for looking after the immigrants who come to* Canada who are desirous of securing positions on the land; and they get two dollars for every person whom they locate on the land.
The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Michaud) spoke about an office located in a town in his constituency. My information is that that office was selected by our travelling inspector, and he claims that it is absolutely necessary for our immigration agent at that point, who is waiting there for the ferries to come in and out, to have some place for shelter in the bad weather, and I suppose he might even sit in the barber shop and await the arrival of the ferries. Occasionally he has to take in an immigrant for examination, and he desires to have some room which he can use as his own. There was a room at the back of the barber shop which he rented for himself for this purpose, paying ten dollars a month, with light, heat and the telephone thrown in. I do not think that is an exorbitant rent. I do not know anything about what the hon. gentleman states, other than, as we are informed by our travelling inspector, that this office is being used. My hon. friend states that it has not been used, but the information in the department is that it has been. I

will, however, make further inquiries and see if the hon. gentleman's allegations are strictly in accord with the information which we have secured.
I have the words of the immigration agent himself that he was not going to use the room because it was not fit to use. He said that he was using a room in his own house as an office.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not suggesting that the immigration agent wishes us to rent his room instead of this office?
I think it would be preferable to do so.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If the agent is looking upon it in that light, I can see that his judgment might not be as impartial as it might otherwise be.
The department should rent a room out of his apartment; he owns a large apartment house.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Beauce (Mr. Beland) and two hon. members on this side of the House referred to the necessity of having our 'boundary inspectors competent to understand and speak bo$h languages. I think that -is very desirable. Most of those boundary inspectors understand French, and speak it, though, in some instances, they may not be able to do so. At those places where the French-Canadians migrate from the United States to Canada, I think, upon the whole, the boundary inspectors understand both languages, although there may be some individual exceptions. It has also been said that we should have a French-Canadian attached to the Boston office. We have a very efficient officer there in the person of Mr. Bowlby, and there are not many French-Canadians in Boston with whom he is brought in contact. We had a report on this subject from our inspector of United States agencies, Mr. White, who reported against the suggestion as unnecessary. We have a French-Canadian, Mr. Laferriere, in charge of the office in Manchester, which is only a few miles from Boston, and he travels through New Hampshire amongst his fellow-countrymen in the endeavour to repatriate as many as he can. I do not know that it is necessary for me to speak longer; I think I have covered, as succinctly as I could, practically all the points which have been brought to my attention.
Can the hon. minister give me the name of the agent at St. Albans?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think it is Mr. Demers.
How many special immigration agents have been operating in the past year from Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman mean; operating where?

In the old country.
I may explain that in the constituency I have the honour to represent, when a disappointed office seeker begins to play the baby act and they have to give him soothing syrup, they make him . either a food inspector or an immigration officer, and he goes over to the old country for three months or so at a salary of $100 a month and expenses. I know one gentleman, a very respectable gentleman, indeed, but not qualified at all by education, experience, or otherwise to be an immigration officer- though a disappointed office seeker-who was sent away for three months, and his expenses were $794 or thereabouts. I think he was supposed to go to the land of my forefathers in the interests of immigration, but I have not seen any of the good sturdy Scotch people coming to the county of Antigonish as the result of his propaganda. What do these gentlemen do for their money-what are the duties of these special immigration officers? Others have been sent from Cape Breton, and I presume with about equal qualifications with those of the gentleman of whom I speak-a very estimable man. Personally I am glad to see him appointed to a position of that kind, because he wanted it. But, so-far as the minister's duty goes, there is no justification for such appointments.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Chisholm) is a little self-contradictory-he is glad to see this gentleman appointed yet says he is useless as an immigration agent. Some of those special agents were sent last year, as formerly, but none have been sent this year. And it is very likely that amongst those who-went from Canada, an odd one may not have been thoroughly qualified for the duty he was supposed to discharge. Still, those immigration delegates have done valuable work in the past. They went over for a length of time, some for two months, some for three months, and a few, I think, for four months, under a salary of $100 a month. This system has been in vogue for many years.

Those agents have acted as lecturers and have given interviews with people there to encourage emigrants to come to Canada. Of course, it is almost impossible to trace the result of each agent's work, but probably all have contributed more or less to the general result attained.
Do these agents report to the department, and are their reports in writing?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
They all report to the
department in writing, I understand.
Is it the intention to send such agents next year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No. I have not sent any this winter, as I do not think it necessary.

The hon. minister has made, I think, a very fair and complete statement as regards the operation of the immigration officials in the different countries, by no means the least being Scotland the country of the forefathers of my hon. friend from Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) whom I am glad to see in his place again. I would like to say a word with regard to immigration from the land of my forefathers, France, and also from Belgium. Had the minister been taking an active part in the political conflicts of the province of Quebec for the last ten or fifteen years, he would have listened to very impassioned appeals against the late Administration for having failed in its duty to bring to Canada more of the sturdy sons of France and Belgium. At that time we answered the attacks made by the friends of the hon. minister by saying that it was an easy matter to appeal to the passions of the people of Quebec, but that one who knew anything about the conditions in France was perfectly aware that a large influx of French immigrants to Canada or any other country in America was almost impossible. We answered our opponents that there were two reasons why the French could not immigrate into America in large numbers. The first was the depopulation in France, due to a decreasing birthrate. The second was, and is, the law of compulsory military service. In France, as in Germany and nearly eveTy other country of Europe, with the honourable exception of Britain, military service is compulsory, and the French authorities are particularly anxious that every young man of that country should serve-some time ago it was two years, and now three 
years-in the army in fulfilment of his legal military obligations. In spite of these obstacles we were none the less taken to task for not attracting more of this immigration. But let bygones be bygones. We, however, got a fair number of excellent French immigrants during the time we were in office. In 1897 and 1898 this immigration was about 300 or 400 a /ear, and in one year, the year after the treaty between France and Canada came into force, it reached highwater mark at over 2,000 immigrants. Since that time the French Government has been dissuading, through its prefects iin various parts of France, the French farmers from emigrating. There, has even been a campaign, quite unjust, waged against Canada on the part of some of the public men in France. But in spite of all that it is, I contend, possible for the Canadian Government to secure, without annoying the French authorities, quite a sprinkling of excellent immigrants from the French farming centres. Looking over the report of the Department of the Interior, I find that our agent in Paris, M. Wiallard, says:
We are using all legitimate means to make Canada known over here in all its aspects, geographical, historical and economic. We have given this year about five hundred lantern lectures, in places where the knowledge of our country was not as yet sufficiently Established, and I am looking forward to an extension of this work. The pictures shown in connection with these lectures exhibit the beauties of our country; our superb rivers, immense lakes, magnificent forests, luxuriant vegetation, our imposing mountains, and our fertile plains, the prairie covered with wheat fields, which are the admiration of all the world. The organization of these lectures kept us well occupied all winter. It has enabled us to distribute about 20,000 atlases and 1,500 wall maps, which, for the most part, are placed on the walls of public schools.
We have had, as in past years, to reply to a number of inquiries coming in from Luxembourg, Switzerland, and the north of Italy, as well as to a great number of persons who, though of foreign nationaity, live in France and wish to go to Canada. Among these are many Belgians.
I was one	of	those who	were	instrumental in securing the appointment of Mr. Wiallard. He is a faithful agent, but I cannot understand how he has been able to give so many lectures in the course of a year, because, with the exception of one or perhaps two sub-agents in his office, he is left practically alone. I would ask my hon. friend to give Mr.	Wiallard such	help	as hemay require	to	encourage,	in whateverway it may	be	encouraged,	the	current
of French immigration towards Canada, As I have said, it ;s not possible -to have a large French immigration into Canada, but .it is possible to secure from the provinces of northern France quite a good sprinkling of peasants. The French peasant is well off, generally speaking, and in the northern part of France, as in the province of Quebec, the members of each family are generally very numerous, which speaks volumes for the honesty of the Frenchman. I may say, en passant, that I have received letters from French settlers in Alberta and Saskatchewan who are doing exceedingly well on their farmis. They, at times, have had some trouble with the agents of the department in those provinces. Whenever I have appealed to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), to my hon. friend the present incumbent, or the officers of his department, Mr. Cory, Mr. Cote and the others, I have always found them most willing to disentangle any of the entanglements which have existed between the French settlers and the authorities. I know, therefore, that my hon. friend is well-meaning, and would be anxious to do anything to favour French immigration. After alland I can say it without boasting

the
Frenchman in Canada has proved himself to be a good settler. The French people who came to this country long before any -of my colleagues' forefathers, early in the sixteenth century, were but a handful. By the census which was taken after the cession *of Canada to Great Britain it was *established that there were only 60,000 Canadians in what was then known as Canada, which extended from the Atlantic to the gulf of Mexico. Less than two centuries afterwards, we find by the census of the United States and the census of Canada that that race, unaided by any stream of' immigration from the old country, has reached the wonderful figure of over 3,000,000. This proves that the Frenchman is essentially a good and desirable settler. I may say to my hon. friend the Postmaster General, to the Deputy Speaker, to the hon. member for Dorchester, and all those who took the Liberals to task when they were in office, that when I was a minister of the Crown I had an interview with the Prime Minister of France, Mr. Briand, about a circular issued by his Government warning the prefects of France that there should be no propaganda for any emigration towards Canada. I said: Why did you issue such a circular; what is the raison d'etre of it?
He said: we are obliged to do it; we are losing heavily every year by the decrease :n the birth rate, besides, we must keep our young men in France, because of our compulsory military service. These were the reasons given by Mr. Briand. It was not because the late Administration was adverse to any French immigration into Canada; on the contrary II think both parties are willing that there should be as much as possible of that immigration from France and Belgium.
The policy of Canada should be to promote immigration, especially from the northern countries of Europe, from the British Isles, from Scandinavia, from the northern portion of France, from Belgium and from that portion of central Europe which comprises Prussia and Austria.
I would like my hon. friend to give a little more help to Mr. Wiallard, who is practically alone in that office in Paris. He should have more literature, more clerks and perhaps a more generous budget.
I leave that to the tender mercies of the minister.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: What would the hon. gentleman think of having our office there merged with the office of Mr. Roy?

That is a question which I shall take up a little later on. One office is in the rue De L'Isly and the other on the boulevard des Capucines. Perhaps it would -be much better if there was one central office in Paris and one advertisement for Canada. You have no idea what the southern countries 'are doing in Paris. Paris is the centre of Europe and it is also with London the great financial centre * of the world. It has been said more than once that France is the banker of the bankers. Therefore there is always attracted to Paris a very large floating population from all parts of the world. And the southern countries, the South American republics, have, for the last twenty-five years, made a tremendous display in Paris. Take, for instance, Brazil, take the Argentine republic, to name but two. My hon. friend the Postmaster General knows that they have made a big display in Paris in order to attract the attention of t'he world to their countries. I do not say that Canada should follow exactly the same policy, but we should, within certain limits, make our country better known from this great centre of Europe, the city of Paris.
One word about Belgium. We can also draw from Belgium quite a large population. The Belgians are an exceedingly interesting people, probably the best farmers and
1G32

the most advanced gardeners in the world. Now that our city population is increasing, in such cities as Toronto and Montreal, we require around the large centres market gardeners. The Belgians are known as the best gardeners in Europe. It is a very desirable population to have in Canada; and you know that in Belgium you have more people per acre than in any other country in the world. The population is congested, is living on a very small territory and yet thanks to its industrious methods, is exceedingly well off. You will have no paupers from France and Belgium. You will have bright people, highly educated, knowing their trade, and familiar with the most scientific methods
9 p.m. of agriculture far better than emigrants coming from any other country in the world. Therefore, it is an emigration to be encouraged. True, it will not come here in very large numbers, but the sprinkling we shall have will certainly be of appreciable economic value to the people of this country. We have an illustration of this in Montreal. During two centuries the farms or rather the gardens around Montreal belonged to the old French-Canadian families. Some of those families became exceedingly wealthy by the cultvation of the land immediately around the city. The lands have passed out of cultivation in the last ten or fifteen years on account of their increased value for residential purposes. We have been fortunate enough to have during the last eight or ten years some Belgian gardeners and, strange to say, some Italians from the northern part of Italy, who have taken up gardening. I may say that, with a much less extended area of territory at their disposal, these Belgians, North of Italy peasants and French gardeners, are making possibly more money than the French-Canadians were .making .around Montreal many years before. Therefore, I repeat, this immigration is a splendid one to attract to this country. I would ask my hon. friend, who I know is well disposed, to give to Mr. Treau de Coeli, the Canadian immigration agent in Brussels, some further help so that he may provide us with a few more Belgian gardeners.
We have had the Social Congress sitting in Ottawa during the last week. Even if we. * had not had the Social Congress we know from good authority that, in spite of our stringent immigration regulations, there is a white slave traffic going on in this country. One has only to read the papers to
	.
learn that there is unfortunately such a traffic going on in this country and in the United States. What steps are taken by the department to prevent that immoral traffic? Has the department any detectives or any special agents to watch over the girls who are coming from the old country? In my judgment the department for several years past, by allowing the delegates of the various churches to attend the immigrants when they reach Quebec, Halifax or any of the other ports of	entry,	has	done indeedexcellent	service	to	the	country.
I would urge upon my hon. friend to give instructions to his agents-whether they travel with the immigrants, or see them at the port of embarkation or port of entry- to exercise a very careful surveillance over young girls coming to Canada. I do not know as much about the other churches as I do about my own church, but I do know that the Salvation Army is doing excellen! work at the gates of our jails when the poor fellows are again sent back to their fellow-men. It is also doing efficient work at the various ports of entry. In Quebec, Reverend Father Casgrain has been appointed. He has served in the British Army in India for many years and speaks several languages. He is familiar with all the dialects of Russia, and consequently can render great service to immigrants coming from different parts of Russia, especially as he is acquainted with their customs and manners.
I have read an excellent pamphlet on immigration written by a member of the press gallery, Mr. Pelletier of Montreal, and printed in Le Devoir. Mr. Pelletier has made a most searching inquiry at Quebec and I think this pamphlet ought to be printed in English. It contains some very interesting data about immigration, and describes the arrival and reception of these immigrants by representatives of the different churches. It is gratifying to know that these foreigners arriving in our country meet in the pastors of the various churches friends ready and willing to help them in their new venture. The pamphlet contains a resume of our immigration policy and methods, and excellent suggestions for the Department of Immigration. I have sat in Parliament nearly twenty years, and have read this pamphlet not only once but twice. It is the best publication on the subject.
Now, about the restrictions that should be imposed on immigration. I know that it is the policy of the Government to prevent as much as possible any congestion in our industrial centres through an influx of immi-

grants. The policy of the Government is to bring farmers to this country. We want farmers, we want navvies, and we want domestics. But we must all ackowledge that in the last few years the population of our rural districts has been decreasing, and that the newcomers instead of settling on the land crowd into the cities. I remember very well that last year there was a large influx of foreigners to Toronto. They were all newcomers who had been trained to the land, but at the approach of winter they flocked to the city and Toronto people had to pay the piper and maintain them durirg the long winter months. 1 mink the same thing has happened th;s year, not only in Toronto but in Montreal and Winnipeg and possibly some other cities. I just wish to quote from an excellent article by Miss Dorothea Brown, published in the Canadian Courier some weeks ago:
There is another phase of this problem equally perplexing. Notwithstanding the fact that the efforts of the Canadian Government are, as we have seen, directed towards securing farmers and farm labourers, we are not increasing the proportion of our people on the land. A comparison of rural and urban population in the United States and Canada will show the tendencies to crowd the cities and magnify the evils of congested districts are practically the same in the two countries. In
1910 53.7 per cent of the population of the United States was rural and 4.63 urban. In
1911	the Canadian population was distributed in the proportion of 5.4 per cent rural and 45.6 per cent urban. The increase in food prices in the United States was 29 per cent, and in Canada 27 per cent. Students of economics and social science are agreed that a nation desiring permanence and stability cannot afford to increase its urban at the expense of its rural population. Only a few years ago 75 per cent of Canada's people were living on the land, or were identified with agricultural pursuits. Today conditions are changing with great rapidity.
The tariff is not solely responsible for the high cost of living; unquestionably the aggregation of large numbers of newcomers within our cities is one of the causes. Is the department doing anything to prevent such flocking to the cities? I would like to know whether my hon. friend intends to take any measures to prevent this aggregation of immigrants in the cities.

Have we any immigration agents in Italy? As the hon. member for Rouville has stated, we are getting a large number of immigrants from Italy. I have not the figures of Italian immigration before me but I know that the minister is familiar with them. We have some very good immigrants coming from Italy. I do not want to make any comparisons but I
think the best immigration is that coming from the north, from Milan, Florence, Taranto and Piedmont generally. Some time ago there was a case at the port of entry of St. Albans in connection with which I had to communicate with the department. I shall not mention the case although I may say here that, according to my information, it was a case coming under the white slave law. Unfortunately, there was some misunderstanding or some error. The facts are these: A young girl, coming from Italy had reached America through the port of New York, had come to a little town in one of the eastern states and was prevented from crossing the border. She lived for a certain number of days, if not weeks, with her brothers in that little town in the United States and a brother of hers living in Montreal wanted to escort her to the city of Montreal. I am not criticising the acts of the officer because the promptitude with-which the case was settled indicated that everything was done that could be done, but in order to prevent such an occurrence I would .suggest that it would 'be a wise policy for the Government to establisn an affioe in- Italy to assist desirable immigrants and to prevent the influx of undesirable immigrants. My hon. friend remembers very well the situation we had in Montreal at one time when a certain employment agent caused a sudden influx of about 10,000 Italians during the winter. A judge of the High Court was appointed to inquire into the matter. This could be prevented in future if we had a permanent office in Italy. If we could come to some arrangement by which no Italian could leave Italy unless he embarked at one or two designated ports, let us say Naples, Genoa or Civita Vecchia, which is the port nearest Rome, we would exercise a large degree of control over that immigration. The resident agent would get familiar with the customs of the country, gather information on the spot and he would not permit the steamship companies to sell tickets to undesirable immigrants, in this way saving trouble and expense to the companies and to the country. My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has referred to the good work that the Reverend Father Cas-grain, the Salvation Army, and ministers of religion generally are doing. T approve that work and no .sensible man could do otherwise. It is worthy of all praise. If we had an office and a resident agent in Italy he could gather information either from the prefect, the mayor of the town or
16.34

the ministers of religion and in this way become acquainted with the mode of living and the latitude in which the prospective immigrants had been brought up because there is a large difference in latitude between the Calabrais on the south and Piedmont in the north and a consequent difference in the character and habits of the people. The man who was appointed specially would become familiar with the habits of the people and after he had been there a short time would probably learn the Italian language. Whether he was a Scotchman, an Irishman or a Frenchman would not matter-the language is .so sweet that with a .little study he would become familiar with it as well as with the manners of the people. We would save money and safeguard the interests of the country if agencies could be established in Italy. Not only would I suggest that we should have an agent in Italy but I would remind the committee that there are no agents on the other side of the Atlantic except those in England and France. Have we any in Russia or Germany? An agent in Germany would surely appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel), because it would prevent undesirable German immigration and it would diminish any fear which may exist of the German peril. Have we any agency in Sweden or Norway? For a comparatively small sum of money we could maintain agents who would render us a great service.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have no agencies in Italy, and I am inclined to think that if we were to establish one it would not meet with the approbation of our Canadian citizens. We do not establish agencies in any countries from which we are not encouraging immigration. We are not encouraging immigration from Italy.

That is not what I mean. I am not ready to say that Italian immigrants are always desirable, but this agency could be established to prevent undesirable persons from coming here. There is no law in this country to prevent an Italian coming, if he is a desirable immigrant.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No; but the point I was going to make was that we would be scarcely justified in establishing immigration agencies in countries to prevent immigration to Canada. That is not the principle upon which we are acting. We are going to the expense of maintaining 
agencies in order to encourage suitable immigrants to come to Canada, but the Italians are usually found segregated in the cities. That is the very condition that my colleague was speaking against a few moments ago. We do not wish to encourage immigrants to make their homes in cities. We are endeavouring to encourage only those who will locate upon the land, and very few Italians go to reside upon the land. With reference to the countries that my hon. friend has spoken about, we have no immigration agency in Germany, and we have none in Norway and Sweden. These countries do not permit us to carry on any immigration propaganda; therefore, it would be idle for us to go to the expense of having officials to prevent immigration from those countries because they are doing their utmost themselves to prevent emigration.
With regard to the illustration that the hon. member gave about a young girl coming across from Italy, landing in the United States, and being prevented by our officer from coming into Canada, I think she would come in in violation of our immigration law. They are supposed to come from the country of their nativity direct to Canada,' and to have the necessary amount of money in their pockets; and by stopping a week in the United States, she could not qualify in that manner and get in under our existing regulations. I quite concur with what the hon. member has stated about the French immigrants. The French peasant makes an excellent settler, and the Belgian peasant as well. We are anxious to see as many as possible of those people come to Canada. We have not a free hand in those countries to carry on our propaganda such as we have in the British Isles. We have to be very circumspect in order to keep within the law. Belgium has not been enforcing her laws very strictly, and perhaps our propaganda has had more freedom there than in France. Our agent in France lias been greatly hampered by reason of the restriction on his work by the laws of that country. Mr. Roy has been urging upon me to centralize our office in his, but I would have to give that matter a little more consideration. I do not know that I could see eye to eye with that proposition. Centralization in some instances is the best policy, but I am inclined to think that our immigration branch in France, in what little we are able to do there, would possibly lose its

identity if merged with the office of Mr. Roy. He is inclined to think that our agent there is possibly liable to get into trouble with the authorities in France, but I am satisfied that the agent, who has been given a good reputation by my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux), is doing good work in so far as he can carry it on, and, if he should step a little beyond the strict regulations and laws of France, he is not doing anything without the consent of the French authorities. I am satisfied as to that. Notwithstanding the fact that we are not allowed to carry on a very strong propaganda in France, I am glad to say that the figures show that we have been getting an increased number year by year. In 1909-10, there were 1,727 immigrants from France; in 1910-11, 2,041; in 1911-12, 2,094; in 1912-13, 2,755. Therefore, we have had some 700 immigrants more from France during the past year than heretofore, and a larger number than ever came to Canada before.	The same
is the case with Belgium. In 1909-10. there were 910 immigrants from Belgium; in 1910-11, 1,563; in 1911-12, 1,601; in 1912-13, 1,826. We are not losing sight of the Belgian and French immigrants. In my own province of Manitoba, there are companies, such as the Million for Manitoba League, who are now endeavouring to encourage Belgian farmers to come out and take up market gardening, in which they are such experts, and to settle on some of the land not far from the city of Winnipeg in order to grow garden products which the city of Winnipeg has to import so largely from the United States.

What proportion of oui immigrants engage in farming or market gardening?
. Mr. ROCHE: I do not know that I could tell my hon. friend on the spur of the moment, although I have no doubt that the great majority of the people coming to Canada have been going on the land. W'e must take into consideration that the various provinces are carrying on a very active propaganda in the motherland, and that the province of Ontario during the past year has had a larger number of immigrants *than any other province in the Dominion. A very large proportion of those brought out by the provincial Government, and of those who came under the jurisdiction of the Dominion authorities, settled upon the laud in Ontario. It is true that some of th-jm may have gone into the cities, but I saw a statement made by a minister in the Ontario legislature that not a single immigrant brought out by the provincial Government to.the province of Ontario during tne past year is to-day without employment. That speaks very well for the immigration to that province. The Dominion Government is encouraging by bonus, only those going on the land, and domestic servants. .
I was glad to hear the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) speak so highly of the -work done by the Salvation Army. The time was, and not so long ago, when the propaganda carried on by the Salvation Army did not meet with such reception. While in the earlier days of the work they may have been open to the accusation of bringing in a certain number of undesirables, they are like the rest of us very anxious to bring desirable immigrants, and they are doing good work and bringing especially those who desire to enter domestic service, as well as those who desire. to go upon the land.
The most of them do not go on the land.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Perhaps not as many ot them go on the land, as those brought in. under the auspices of the Dominion Government, I understand from Commissioner Lamb that they bring no one out here without'having assured employment.

The remarks which 1
made about the Salvation Army do not apply so much to the work they may be doing outside of Canada to induce immigrants to come here. I do not know much about that phase of the work. I was simply eulogizing the work of the Salvation Army at the ports of entry, how they take care of the people, how they guide them, and how they promote the good cause-amongst the immigrants. They really do-take good care of them and they are good friends. Thdt was what I was referring to.
Mr, NESBITT: Has the hon. minister any machinery for keeping track of emigration? We hear about immigration, but we: have no record that I know of with reference to emigration. The number of people coming to Canada would build up our population more, rapidly than the census shows, and I for one think that the business community would like to have a knowledge of how many people go away from the country. According to the American return, that the hon. member for Edmonton read this afternoon, nearly as many people went back to the United States as came from

there last year and the year before. We should not depend entirely upon the American figures for that information. Could not the hon. minister establish machinery in his department for keeping track of the people who leave the country as well as of the people who come in? That would be of great benefit to the business men of this country.
With reference to the Salvation Army, my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) is quite right as to the care they take of our immigrants; but most of the men whom they bring out stay in the towns. The domestic servants they bring out supply a very great need.

Up to the present time
there has not been any real system of compiling statistics of persons going from Canada, but I do not think that the hon. member was present, when I read a reply from the department to the allegation made in th,e American press.

I was not in at that
time.
I placed that upon ' Hansard.' The figures are entirely incorrect. We made a special investigation and satisfied ourselves on that point.
I am glad to hear that.

The question under discussion is one of very great interest to the country and of-peculiar interest to the district from which I come. That district has already been referred to by the hon. Minister of the Interior when he spoke of that part of the province of Ontario which had undertaken a campaign of immigration locally, and apart from the Government. This campaign was undertaken because the provincial Government realized the absolute necessity of peopling the country districts with labourers. We have the hydro-electric question, which is a live question amongst the farmers; we have the Farmers' Institute, agricultural societies and other advantages which add interest to the agricultural community, and which, it was hoped, might tend to increase the interest of the young men and hold them on the farm. But, after carefully viewing the whole situation, our farmers in that district commenced to realize that there is no subject of more importance to them than that of being able to get satisfactory labour to assist them on the farm. I listened with great interest to the debate this afternoon. I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Eouville (Mr. Lemieux) that

it is of great importance that our immigration propaganda should be waged in those countries of Europe where agriculture is brought to the highest state of perfection and where we may hope to get men of intelligence, trained in the work of the farm and likely to follow that avocation after they come here. The question has been asked:	How do we know how many of
these immigrants from the Old country go on the farm? In the campaign of publicity carried on last year by the district from which I come, although that was the first year in which we engaged in that	work, we know that we
really put more people into the country districts of that community than during any other five years in our history. The campaign was so thoroughly satisfactory that the county of Middlesex itself, this year, without assistance from the Government, has engaged in the work and has sent a man to the agricultural districts of the old country to engage the farm labour that we require and send it out to us. I am very strongly of opinion that if that line of endeavour were followed out by all the the counties throughout the Dominion they would be entitled to assistance from the Dominion Government in the work. I believe that local effort in that direction with the co-operation of the Dominion Government would probably bring effective results distributed well throughout all parts of the country. Eeference has been made to the commissioners of immigration that the department sent to the old country last year. I do not know anything about the results that were attained by the efforts of the majority of these men, but I have a personal knowledge of the results from the labour of the man who left the district from which I come. His work was so effective and the class of immigrants sent through his efforts so satisfactory to the people of our community that when we came this year to send to the old country for that purpose, we selected the very man whom the Government selected last year, and he is now on the ocean on his way over to work along the same line.
I do not wish to take up time unnecessarily, but I desire to say a word with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). His remarks and the deductions he drew from certain figures of the blue book, led me to think there might be some other cause than that which he gave for the increase in the number of deportations. While the minister has answered well the comparison between 1911

and 1913, might it not have been as well to go back to the year 1907 and compare conditions? In my opinion, the fact that the deportations have increased during a financial stringency does not necessarily imply laxity on the part of the Government in admitting these people into the country. There is no congestion of labour in the country districts; we know that the country is able to absorb an enormous number of labourers at the present time. But at the same time, there is a congestion of labour in the industrial community. Is it not natural to suppose that at such a time the Government would use a little more than ordinary vigilance to prevent the further congestion of labour? When I heard the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton, they led me to look back to 1907 and study the figures of that year. There were 825 deportations, as the hon. member stated. The deduction that the hon. member drew from an increase in the number of deportations was that the Government had not exercised proper vigilance in examining the immigrants coming in. I examined the reasons for deportation in the years 1907-8, and found, they were as follows:
Tuberculosis	 70
Rheumatism	 20
Defective eyes	 6
Insane	122
Feeble-minded	 13
Epilepsy and locomotor ataxia ..	14
Old age crippled and deaf	 15
Likely to become a public charge.. 279 Criminal prostitute and vagrancy..	98
From other causes	187
If the argument of the hon. gentleman is right as to 1913, it applies equally to 1907-8. If proper-no, I will not say that, because it is not the word-if absolute care had been exercised in the examination of these immigrants, we should not have had to deport 122 insane, 15 feeble-minded and 70 affected with tuberculosis. I have no doubt that, no matter what care the department may exercise, it is impossible to prevent some undesirables from coming in. But I do say the Government has shown proper vigilance in deporting these people. I do not care whether the number be 800 or 2,000. In the year 1907-8, as I have said, the figures show a decrease in the deportations. But I went back also to the period from 1902 to 1907, to see how closely the immigrants were examined and how many were deported during those years of prosperity. 525 immigrants were deported during that period. In the succeeding year, the first year of the financial stringency of that time, the deportations increased 63 per cent.
The following year they jumped from 825 to 1,748. The immigrants we want are those in the agricultural districts of the old country which have been brought up to the highest state of cultivation. If we want mechanics, we go where we find mechanics who have made good; if we want to get good farmers, we must get them from those districts in the old land or in Europe where agriculture has been brought up to a high state of efficiency. If they are good men, it matters not whether they are f-om Belgium, Denmark, or any of those countries the citizens of which can assimilate with those of our country and become good Canadians. I am very strongly of the opinion, and I hope the minister will give this his most serious consideration-I have already discussed the matter with him personally-that the probabilities of co-operating with the communities themselves in sending able men as commissioners to the old land are very great. In my humble opinion, very effective work can be done through the co-operation of the department with the individual localities in following up the propaganda that we have undertaken in the county of Middlesex. Of course we do not want to localize the matter to any considerable extent; we should realize that we are doing what is best for the country at large. Any man sent to the old country as the representative of any community, if he were being paid or assisted by that community, and even by the Government, would feel a greater responsibility to that community to make good than he would feel as a commissioner selected to represent the country at large. Some of the men who may be attracted from the old land to our district this year are bound to find their way into the other counties, but we have no petty jealousies or ill-feeling about that; we feel that we will get a sufficient number of them to make it worth the expenditure to which we are subject in carrying the idea into effect.

Have the people of my
hon. friend's county nau any experience in bringing these men to Canada, and if so, what has been their experience with regard to emigrants staying where they were first placed?

Our experience is only in
its initial stage; we have had only one year of it. I asked the department what would be the most effective way of making the pamphlet which we issue of such a nature as to increase interest in the idea of coming to our district. I was told, and I believe, rightly, that the best way to adver-

liise a community in the old land is to (jive an honest, plain story of the man who has come out to settle on the land and has made good. A number of persons came into our district last year, and we have been obtaining letters from them telling in their own way-we do not dictate it; we want the story in their own words- the success with which they have met, and we propose publishing a number of these and circulating them in connection with the other literature. We have not statistics or figures to show how many of these men have stayed where they were first placed, but we have a number of letters from those who did stay, saying that they had intended to stay only six months or a year, but had been used so well that they had made up their minds to stay two or three years. I have had personal letters from a number of agriculturists in the old country who wished to come out here, men who are wording on a couple of acres of land and earning eighteen or twenty-five shillings a week. It is impossible for them, with that small wage, to get together enough money to bring them to this country. In Middlesex they are suggesting a plan by which a guarantee fund will be put up and the money advanced to these men-I mean men of good character, men of experience, men whom it is desirable to bring to this country-to pay their trans. portation expenses and bring them to Canada. In not less than a dozen instances the farmers paid the entire expenses of men coming out here, and I am told that in every case the services given are satisfactory and the men are making good. If I were looking for a man from the old country who would make good on the farm, I would say that the man who is now working on a farm, raising a family of four or five children, and living in a little home and making eighteen or twenty shillings a week, would be a frugal, careful man, and would make a desirable citizen of this country. I would not care whether he had capital or not; if he had experience and was a man who could take care of a large family on that amount, he would be a desirable citizen of a country like this, where, the land is so free and the crops so abundant.
I hope that the scattered remarks I have made, and the little experience we have had along these lines, may result in something being done in the future, and that the Government and individual communities may co-operate to solve, at least to some extent, the problem of farm labour.
[Mr. Glass 1

My opinion is that our immigration policy is all wrong. I have said this every session during which I have been in Parliament. I think it is a crying shame that 1.500 poor people who have paid their passages across the ncean to come to this country should be deported. I have pleaded with the late Government, asking that the inspection should be made on the other side, and the only reason why it is not done is because of the terrible question of patronage. One or two doctors in London, Liverpool, and Southampton would prevent the condition under which 1,500 poor people, after paying some $50,000 to come to this country, are turned back shortly after landing in Canada.
I am speaking now from a purely humanitarian standpoint. Is it not a fact that every year numbers of poor people pay their steamship fares to Canada, and after they get here perhaps your doctors find that they are not fit to come into the country? I am not finding fault with that; the fault I find is that you do not have the inspecting done on the other side of the ocean instead of here. Many times, and I am sure the minister or his deputy would know of it, families have been broken up; sometimes the mother has been discovered to have trachoma and has had to go back, either taking her children with her or leaving them here; the family is broken up in any case; -and all because the inspection is not done on the other side. 1 do hope that the present minister will remedy this. Two years ago I pleaded with the minister of that day, now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), and I understood the matter was to be considered. I also brought the matter before Mr. Scott, superintendent of immigration. Is there any good reason why these fifteen hundred poor families should come out to this country at a cost of some $45,000 or $50,000 and then be turned back?
In what sense are you using the word poor; is it with reference to their poverty?
Yes.
Or is it poor in the sense of being physically unfit?

I say they are
unfortunate, and many of them are in poverty. Some of them can barely get enough money together to pay their passage out here.

Does the hon. gentleman think that this inspection should bo made

by the steamship company or by the Canadian Government?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Oh, yes, they do.
They have to take them back.

Yes, if you catch
them. Is there any common sense in bringing these people to this country if they have not the $25, or have some mental or other disease that compels them to be sent back? There is not a member in this House who would take the ground that there is any good reason for allowing these people to come out here, and then send them back. They lose their situations and break up their families in the old country, all because we want to have the
10 p.m. medical examiners on this side.
Send three or four doctors to the other side and stop them from getting aboard, not only because of disease, but for any other reason that would prevent them entering Canada,

The hon. gentlefnan advises the minister to^ send doctors across to England, Scotland or France to prevent these people from getting on board ship. I doubt very much if this Government would have authority to send a man to England, to France, or to any other country to say who should or should not get on board a vessel.

Of all the reasons 1 have - yet heard that is the poorest one. Every man in this House knows that if the Government asked the British Government to let them put a doctor or two at Liverpool, that privilege would be granted immediately, The hon. gentleman knows that as well as I do.
The steamship companies would listen to them.

Everybody would
listen to them. I said the same thing to the former Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver). For many years I have pleaded for that and it has got to come whether it comes immediately or not. People will not stand for these poor people being robbed as they are in this matter. If the reason advanced by the hon. member for Frontenac is the only one, the minister could fix it in five minutes.

In such a matter as that each country would have jurisdiction over its own ports. My hon. friend is assuming entirely too much when he assumes that this Government could, in all the various countries from which Canada receives immigrants, appoint -its agents to stand at the ports and say who should and who should not get on board a vessel.

Does the hon. gentleman not think that other countries would welcome it, rather than have their poor people sent over here and then have them sent back again ? Every country in the world from which we receive immigrants, will welcome it.

On the contrary, instead of these countries welcoming such officials, the very fact that so many of these people com.ing from various countries have to be deported, shows an inclination on the part of these countries to get rid of them. They are only too glad to get rid of them.
Not at all.

The hon. member for
the St. Lawrence division of Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) is anxious that the medical inspection of immigrants should be performed at the sailing port. I agree with him that such a system would be the best, but before accepting the suggestion it may be advisable to look over the report of the United States commission of immigration, a report which I have quoted the other day in the following terms:
It is highly desirable both for humanitarian and medical reasons that aliens who are not admissible to the United States should be turned back at foreign ports of embarkation, or better still, that they should not leave their homes for such ports only to be returned. It has been strongly urged by immigration officials and other students of the question that the embarkation at foreign ports of persons not admissible to the United States because of their physical condition, would be more effectually prevented by a medical inspection by American officers at such ports. This plan was so strongly urged that this Government a few years ago made official inquiry respecting the probable attitude of European governments toward it. At that time one or two governments expressed a willingness to permit such an inspection by American officials; others made indefinite replies to the inquiry, while others were positively opposed.
Such are findings of the United States commissioners appointed to inquire into the conditions in the various European countries. Now, I requested the Minister of the Interior a few days ago, to co-operate

with the imperial authorities so as to obtain that right of inspection at ports of embarkation.
Is not the hon member wholly agreeable to the proposal of effecting the inspection on the other side of the Atlantic rather than in our seaports?

I am in favour of making a selection as judicious as possible of the immigrants. I believe that one of the means of preventing the deportation of undersirables would be to have the inspection made at the sailing ports, or on 'the ships carrying the immigrants. A few days ago, I stated that, in my humble opinion, the ideal system would be to have the medical inspection performed by a specialist appointed and paid by the Canadian Government on board the ships carrying the immigrants.
But why not previous to their boarding the ship ?

For this reason: We must first find out whether we have jurisdiction in foreign lands and, from what I have read, we have no such jurisdiction in foreign countries. It appears from the report of the United States commission which I have just referred to, that the United States experts offer merely suggestions which are, it is true, generally complied with by foreign governments.
In Europe generally things are done in this way. Let us take Germany, for instance. Russians and Austrians wish to cross the German frontier with a view to reaching a German seaport and thence cross over to America. On the German frontier, there are stations for the medical inspection of immigrants, and no undesirables are allowed to proceed any further.
On Monday last, I stated further that in Greece there are stations for medical inspection in their own towns. Besides, the [DOT]other day, I referred to the means that should be taken to prevent as much as possible the hardships inflicted by deportation. It is apparent that the medical officer at the port of embarkation has not enough time at his disposal to detect mental or constitutional diseases with which the immigrant may be afflicted. If inspection was performed on the ship by an expert appointed and paid by the Canadian Government, he might during the trip take the requisite time and means to have the immigrants undergo such an inspection as I believe to be necessary in the country's interest
The hon. gentleman advocates inspection on the ocean, on board the vessels. But no ship would turn around when half way across the sea to take back a rejected immigrant.
He means to chuck them overboard.

You might as well leave the inspection until you get to this side, as to have the inspection half way across the ocean, because no vessel will turn back if they discover smallpox or trachoma when they are at sea. There is only one way, and my hon. friend will agree that the best way is to do the inspecting on the other side.

I will agree with my hon. friend who has just spoken to the extent of wishing that it were possible to mitigate the horrors of deportation or even of rejection. I would be willing to support the Administration in going to very great lengths to mitigate the conditions that exist at the present time, that, under the system that now prevails, must exist. They are just as deplorable as my hon. friend has suggested, and in the interests of humanity they should be avoided so far as possible. I am afraid with all my hon. friend's goodness of heart-and nobody will say he has not a large measure of that-I think he lacks, if I may criticise, to some extent, the principle of charity in considering the views and limitations of other people; and he has perhaps not considered in all its bearings the difficulties that surround his proposition. At the same time there is a deplorable condition. I am sure the minister himself must have felt that when cases have been brought to his attention, and I am sure that he would wish, as I would wisa, to see that condition mitigated as far as possible. I would be glad if the Government would take such measures as on full consideration may seem possible to secure a mitigation of the miseries resulting from the necessary strict enforcement of the law in regard to rejection and deportation. I would be willing as a member of the Opposition to give him a free hand in such an endeavour and I would certainly commend it strongly to the minister that he take consideration of the representations made by my hon. friend to go so far as he can.

Does my hon. friend not think it would be possible to have the inspection done on the other side? I know it would not be easy for any person to do, and because it is hard we are asking the minister himself to find a way of doing it.

I do not need to take time to-night to argue that point. I do not say that the difficulties in the way cannot be overcome. I am putting myself in the position, as a member of the Opposition, of giving the minister a free h'and ip undertaking to overcome these difficulties, which I recognize to a degree which probably my hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdike) does not recognize. Those difficulties may possibly be overcome and I would he glad to see the minister take the opportunity of overcoming them so far as he can. Nothing caused me more difficulty of mind during the time I had charge of the Immigration Department than this matter of deportation and rejection, but I felt that the interests of the country demanded that there should be a policy of restriction and selection. Parliament vested that authority in me and, unpleasant though it was, I felt that I was compelled to do my duty as it was laid down. In the light of subsequent events it may- be possible to do better now than was done then, and I will be glad to see the minister do better if it is possible to be done. I will join with my hon. friend on this occasion.
It is the first time.

Never too late to mend.
I will join with my hon. friend on this occasion, and urge on the favourable consideration of the Government some effort to mitigate those conditions.
In regard to the more general question that was up for consideration in the early part of the discussion,
I wish to say that I am very much pleased at the announcement made by the minister that the lid is on definitely at any rate for the season 1914. I think he has taken a very proper course in deciding that there shall be no relaxation of the regulations during this season and he is entitled to every credit for having taken due measures at the proper time. In regard to his explanation as to the number of people going from Canada to the United States, it is to he regretted that the information is not more definite, hut still it is measurably satisfactory to know that the conditions are not as represented in the returns of the United States Government. I will say, however, that the information that was given indicates a situation that is still somewhat serious. If my memory is correct, my hon. friend mentioned that some 800 cases were investigated, 400 of which were found to be people who had returned or were returning to Canada. If that meant that of the 800 eases investigated, 400 were
really emigrants to the United States, it means that there is a drift of people to the United States much larger than we had any idea of. I would suggest that the matter be gone into more fully so that we can see justwhatour position is in this matter of the coming and going of population.
In regard to the better financial condition of the people coming from the United States,	my hon. friend
said that although fewer homesteads were taken up he had reason to believe that there were more land purchases. I will he glad if that is the case, but again the reports do not indicate it.
I find that the land sales by the different land-owning companies in the West, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1913, are only $9,867,000 as against $18,000,000 for the year before, and that again is nearly a million dollars less than the sales of the year before that-the year ended March 31, 1911. The records are against the supposition of my hon. friend. I would be very glad if it turns out not to be the case, but I am speaking from the record of the department as I find it.
I wish to say that the reason given by my hon. friend for the lessening in the number of homestead entries, if it be correct, and I am not going to controvert his view at the moment, that we have reached highwater mark in our record of homestead entries and that our available homesteads in the West are practically exhausted, means that our position as a field for immigration has undergone a radical change, and it will .be necessary for us to adjust our efforts in regard to immigration in accordance with that new condition. Until the present time, the basic idea of our immigration effort has been to secure the occupation of available vacant land in the Northwest. All other features of our immigration policy merely followed upon that one. If that feature has been either eliminated or minimized, it means that our whole theory of immigration has been changed and it will be necessary to change our system accordingly. If we have not that field for immigrants, then there is no reason for pursuing the policy of inducing such immigrants to come. It is a matter to be considered whether, if the condition is as my hon. friend suggested, we should revise our whole attitude and view. If wo have no more free land available, but if the field now lies in the development of land already occupied, this new condition looks to the securing of a different class

of immigrants. The class of immigrants that occupies the free land is one class, but the class of immigrants that furnishes labour upon land already occupied is another class, and we would have to adjust our immigration efforts and policy accordingly.
The other serious feature I spoke of, and which the minister dealt with, was the large increase in immigration from southern Europe. It is a fact that the immigration of certain classes of people from northern Europe would be a means of strengthening and improving our nationality. It is just as true that a serious influx of .people from southern Europe would he to the detriment of our nationality. Not that these people are not just as good as we are, ibut their social ideals, their ideas of Government, their ideas of living generally, are different from ours, and their presence in large or dominant numbers would mean that our national life would undergo a substantial revision or change. As far as present lines are concerned it would be weakened and not strengthened. My hon. friend says: Yes we are receiving an increased number of these southern European people; but we are not responsible for it; there are certain regulations provided, and if these people comply with those regulations they are, of course, entitled to come in; we make no endeavour to bring them here; they come of their own accord; if they comply with the regulations we must let them in, and there is nothing more for us to do. I do not know what -view my 'hon. friend and the Government may take, but if it is admitted that a large influx of people having different racial characteristics different social ideals, different views in regard to matters of government, is undesirable and if our present regulations are not sufficient for preserving the conditions as we would wish them to be, it is necessary that the Government should make provision to protect those racial characteristics, those ideals of social life and of government that we have at the present time, and Which it is our ambition to perpetuate. The Government is responsible in this matter, and the -country looks to the Government to safeguard it in this as in other particulars.
It is very flattering to the late Government to find that their policy has been adopted and their administration followed up in matters of immigration, and if conditions. remained the same I would have
fMr. Oliver.]
thought, certainly, that the -Government would he well advised in undertaking that course, but if conditions have radically changed, as my hon. friend intimates, they have, in regard to the measurahle exhaustion of the free land on the prairies of the West on the one hand, and an influx of uninduced southern European people on the other hand, steps should be taken to meet those conditions whatever they may be.
I was struck by what my hon. friend from East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) said, in drawing a comparison between the rapid increase of deportations in 1908 as compared with 1907, and 1913 as compared with 1912. He said that the large deportations in 1908 and 1913 were no doubt due to the recurrence of a financial stringency. That is no doubt a fact, and is exactly why I criticised the Government for the condition existing. In 1907, we had a somewhat parallel condition to that prevailing to-day. We had had a period of rapid expansion and prosperity succeeded by a financial depression which threw a great many people out of work. The difference is, that in 1907 we had not adopted the policy of selection, restriction and direction that was embodied in the Act of 1910, and that was in full force and effect when the present Administration took office. It was because of the experience of 1907 and 1908 that we were led to the conclusion that it was necessary to adopt a restrictive, selective and directive policy. We provided by legislation and regulations to that end. We left that law and those regulations in operation when we went out of office. My judgment, based on the experience of 1907, is that our friends did not carry out those regulations; did not live up to the spirit of that Act-were impressed rather with the desire of having a large number than with maintaining the high quality that the Act contemplated; and that it was only when circumstances changed; when it was seen, as it must have been seen, that a mistake had been made, they undertook to repair the mistake by enforcing the provisions of the law very stringently. In the light that they had, with the law and the regulations in their hands, matters should not have reached that point, when it would have been necessary to make such heavy deportations and such large exclusions. That is the criticism I make.

Does the hon. member make due 'allowance for that stringency being the cause of emigration from European countries? The financial stringency

which was felt in this country and on this continent was also felt in England and other European countries, thus driving men out of employment there more than ordinarily. Would not that act as a predisposing cause to increased emigration of the poorer classes?

I have no explanation
that would lead me to that conclusion. On the contrary although I have heard it stated in the House several times that conditions in Great Britain were depressed as they were in this country, that, on my information, is not by any means the fact. I have recently seen in one of the leading London papers an official report stating that employment was never as brisk in Great Britain as it was during the summer of 1913; therefore, so far as the British Isles are concerned, there would be no condition that would force labour to Canada. In regard to continental Europe, certainly so far as the Balkan countries were concerned, instead of men coming from these countries as they did in former yeaTS, the men who had come in former years had gone back to fight the battles of their country, mak-. mg a very serious inroad into the actual working population of our country. My information, therefore, would not bear out the suggestion made by my hon. friend.
The Government was impressed with the idea that it was well that we should have a big immigration, and they lifted the lid; the immigration came and they had to shut the lid down. It was unfortunate that they should have had to do so. It would have been still more unfortunate if they had not done so; but the unfortunate condition was in my opinion the result of an error on their part, and I hope it will not occur again.
Is the minister able to give the House any information as to what course the Government intends to pursue in regard to the matter dealt with in the Order in Council of the 8th of December, 1913?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Before the -end of this
month we will take some action. The matter is under consideration, but if has not yet been definitely decided what action will be taken.	[DOT]
In Tegard to the query of the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) I would direct his attention to section 45 of the Immigration Act:
Every person who does in Canada, anything for the purpose of causing or procuring the publication or circulation, by advertisement or
otherwise, in a country outside of Canada, of false representations as to the opportunities tor employment in Canada, or as to the state of the labour market in Canada, intended or adapted to encourage or induce or to deter or prevent, the immigration into. Canada of persons resident in that country, or who does anything in Canada for the purpose of causing or procuring the communication to any resident of such country of any such false representations, shall, if any such false representations are thereafter so published, circulated or communicated, be guilty of an offence against the Act, and liable, on summary conviction before two justices of the peace, to a penalty for each offence of not more than five -hundred dollars or to imprisonment for not more than six months.
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman, when he asked that question, had in mind the circular read by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) this afternoon, a circular which I stated I had not previously seen. [DOT] If any such advertisement has been inserted in any newspaper in any country, it has been the practice of the department to notify that paper that it is not in accordance with our Immigration Act, and there has never been any difficulty in having the paper cut out such an advertisement. I would like to have the circular in order that we may take whatever action is necessary.

I had in mind the same circular. I was referring to a copy of it, and I probably made a mistake in sending back my reply. I thought that, if the labour bureau -sent men over to Germany, Russia, Italy or any country and make no false representations, they could import labour provided the labourers when they came in had the required fifty dollars, or whatever the amount may be. As I understand the Act. they were not allowed to advertise at all.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, but they were not to make false representations.

That is exactly the
answer I gave, and I wanted to know from the minister that it was correct. While I should be sorry to see immigrants brought in through false representations, yet there is a condition in that part of the country that requires their bureau to act and bring in labour. As I read the circular there was no false representation with regard to wages. As a matter of fact, in the mines of Cape Breton wages are much above those cited. Helpers in the mines get $1.80 and $2 f day. However, that is the answer I gave, though I did not find in tne Immigration Act exactly what the minister read. Still, misrepresentations have been made during

labour troubles. I brought a case to the attention of the House last year, and I am sorry to say that at that time the minister was away on account of illness. Hon. members will recall the case as that of the photo-engravers in Toronto. These men represented to me and to other members on this side of the House, and probably first to the Government, that labour was being imported under false representations for the purpose of breaking the strike. I brought to the attention of the Acting Minister of the Interior-the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) I think it was-the provision of the Immigration Act under which the department may make regulations forbidding the coming into the country during labour troubles or strikes of the kind of labour affected. I think I am within the mark when I say that during troubles between capital and labour the department should bring that regulation into effect.
